title: Mandatory Access to IoT Data under the EU Data Act: A Regime in Conflict with its Purpose
affiliations: Max Planck Institute for Innovation and Competition

detail.title: Mandatory Access to IoT Data under the EU Data Act: A Regime in Conflict with its Purpose

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Max Planck Institute for Innovation & Competition Research Paper No. 26-12
publicationDetails.journalName: Max Planck Institute for Innovation & Competition Research Paper Series

affiliations.org_name: Max Planck Law - Max Planck Institute for Innovation and Competition

detail.abstract: The EU Data Act aims at enhancing data sharing and data-driven innovation activities by fostering the emergence of liquid, fair and effective markets for non-personal data. At the center of the Act is a regime of mandatory access to IoT data. These are data that in the world of the Internet of Things a user generates when using a connected product or related service. The data are digital representations of information that may concern the use of the product or related service or its environment; it can be used for diverse purposes (multifunctionality). Instead of introducing some form of a data-specific property regime, the legislature systematically relies on contract as the basis for allocating control over the use of such data. To this end, the Act confers upon the user, whether industrial firm or end-consumer, an unrestricted statutory privilege to contractually consent or not to consent to the use of the data by other parties (including the data holder); this requirement is enforceable only inter partes. At the same time, the Act legally recognizes the control that the data holder de facto exercises over the product data, and that it may enforce by legally protected technical protection measures. That division of the powers of control between the user and the data holder results in an asymmetry, because, in principle, the user may grant third parties access to the data only via requesting the data holder to make the data available by way of an agreement that the designated third party must negotiate with the data holder. The regulatory concept is one of a triangular relationship with distributed roles, where the user and the data holder are placed in mutually dependent positions, and where third parties, potential competitors of the data holder, are caught in between the user’s and the data holder’s positions. The complexity of this regulatory concept is compounded by ambiguities concerning the user’s role and the basis and function of its consent privilege, and by the frictions that result from non-compete rules, trade secret protection and the protection of personal data. It is, however, not only the dependencies, asymmetries and frictions that stand in the way of the Data Act attaining its objectives. Rather, it is the very concept of regulating the market by attributing market actors functionally predetermined roles instead of tradable rights based on meritorious effort and achievement, which systematically impairs the emergence of liquid and effective markets. On top of it comes the Act’s systematic dissimulation of the subject matter that determines the economic use and value of data: the information they represent. They represent it in digital form, which facilitates the processing and dissemination of the information and, in these ways, enhances its use potential; there is no other function or effect to the digital form. Still, the connecting factor for the application of the Act is precisely this form alone, irrespective of what it covers. However, where the form may cover up substance, fair markets will not emerge.

title: Today's Firms, Tomorrow's Workers: The Aggregate Local Effects of Firm Entry
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Today's Firms, Tomorrow's Workers: The Aggregate Local Effects of Firm Entry

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: There has been growing empirical evidence that job and firm creation generates earnings and employment spillovers into the local labor market. ? found that, in the United States, each additional manufacturing job created in a city was associated with 1.6 jobs created in the non-tradable sector.1 ? found that changes in employment opportunities in a high paying sector affects the wages in other sectors through general equilibrium wage effects; these spillovers are driven by the employment share for a sector and the wage premium.2 When looking at the effects from increased firm entry, ? and ? found economically significant increases in per capita GDP and employment, respectively. Despite evidence showing earnings and employment spillovers from increased entry, the underlying industries driving these results is understudied and the entry effects may be heterogeneous across the industry or sector of entry. One potential source of heterogeneity is whether the firm operates in the tradable or the non-tradable sector (?). The goal of this work is to determine how increased entry in the tradable and non-tradable sectors affects the per capita personal income, unemployment rate, and aggregate employment of a city, how those effects differ across the two sectors, and how these effects evolve over the short, medium, and long runs. Firms in these sectors differ in several important ways. Firstly, firms in the tradable and non-tradable sectors differ in where they can sell their output. A firm operating in the tradable sector can produce their good or service in a city 𝑖 and sell their output either in city 𝑖 or an outside city 𝑗. Differently, a firm in the non-tradable sector that produces their good or service in city 𝑖 must sell their output in that same city 𝑖. 3 Thus, firms in the tradable sector have a much larger geographic range over which they can sell their goods and services. Secondly, firms in the tradable and non-tradable sectors differ in the control they have over their output price (??). Due to not having the ability to sell outside of the city of production, firms in the non-tradable sector are able to adjust their prices to local economic conditions. Differently, firms in the tradable sector take their output price as given as prices are set on the national market. Thirdly, employment in the non-tradable sector depends on local demand while employment in the tradable sector depends on national or global demand (?). Fourthly, industries in the tradable sector have a higher wage premium compared to the non-tradable sector (?).4 Lastly, as shown in Figure 1 and discussed in greater detail below, there is far more variability in the change in entry between years in the tradable sector compared to the non-tradable sector. Because of the differences in where firms are able to sell their output, the pricing decisions available to firms, and the variability in the rate of entry, there may exist differences in the spillovers generated from entry in the tradable sector compared to entry in the non-tradable sector.

detail.abstract: A boutique advisory firm serving taxable clients can run tax-aware mandates in-house, with lot-level control in every account, or allocate to outside managers and accept the fund wrapper's tax pass-through. We price the after-tax wedge between the two through its three channels: the extra fee layer, fund-level gain realizations the client cannot time, and the harvesting a pooled fund forgoes. Behind it sits a closed form for after-tax wealth under partial annual realization, and for the share of a marginal alpha point that survives each wrapper, paired with a fixed-seed Monte Carlo calibrated to a century of Ken French data. Under identical gross returns, and with a liquidation exit, the in-house route ends twenty years 1.8 to 2.0 times wealthier after tax: a wedge of 327 to 404 bp a year across accounts from $250k to $25M. The break-even outside alpha is 235 to 441 bp at liquidation and 416 to 722 bp under a step-up. Four return processes and split-conformal intervals leave the wedge intact. Harvesting is another matter. Below about $1M it is not an identified claim for one client, and the hurdle re-solved on the median runs 80 to 90 bp lower than the mean-based figure.

title: The Willing Buyer, Willing Seller Model: Foreign Exchange Reforms and Stock-Market Dynamics in Nigeria
affiliations: Central Bank of Nigeria, Central Bank of Nigeria, Central Bank of Nigeria and Central Bank of Nigeria

detail.title: The Willing Buyer, Willing Seller Model: Foreign Exchange Reforms and Stock-Market Dynamics in Nigeria
detail.abstract: This study examines whether Nigeria’s transition to the willing-buyer, willing-seller (WBWS) foreign-exchange framework altered the relationship between the naira/US-dollar exchange rate and stock-market performance. Using monthly data on the Nigerian All-Share Index (ASI) and the nominal exchange rate, the analysis combines descriptive evidence with an autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) framework that distinguishes the average exchange-rate–equity relationship from any change associated with the post-WBWS period. The specification includes a regime indicator and its interaction with the exchange rate, while the ARDL bounds approach is used to assess long-run relationships and short-run adjustment. The results indicate a positive long-run association between naira depreciation and the nominal ASI in the baseline model. However, once the WBWS regime and the interaction term are introduced, neither the level shift nor the change in exchange-rate sensitivity is statistically distinguishable from zero, and evidence of stable long-run adjustment becomes weaker. The findings therefore do not support the view that the post-2023 increase in the ASI can be attributed independently to the WBWS reform. Economically, the positive exchange-rate–equity association may reflect nominal asset repricing, the higher naira value of foreign-currency earnings and assets, and portfolio reallocation during periods of currency weakness, while potentially masking adverse effects on import-dependent firms and those with foreign-currency liabilities. The study concludes that the reform should be assessed primarily through improvements in foreign-exchange market functioning rather than nominal equity appreciation alone, while recognising the limits imposed by the short post-reform window and the use of an aggregate market index.

title: On Why Agencies Should Measure Anticompetitive Effects in Merger Control
affiliations: Compass Lexecon

detail.title: On Why Agencies Should Measure Anticompetitive Effects in Merger Control
detail.abstract: Measuring harm can improve merger decisions even when transaction-specific efficiencies remain unobserved. I study a sequential game in which an agency commits to a deterministic approval rule and informed firms decide whether to incur filing and completion costs. Building on Metcalfe, Sollaci and Syverson (2026), private viability raises expected efficiencies at a given harm level, although expected efficiencies can fall with harm across viable transactions. Selection raises the optimal approval threshold only when it excludes lowefficiency types at the original boundary. This conclusion extends beyond uniform distributions and linear private returns. The analysis distinguishes viability from filing, deterrence from rejection, and welfare losses from error frequencies. Its policy implication is to use harm evidence consistently in assessing expected consumer benefits, while accounting for filing incentives and other sources of private value.

title: Randomized to Opportunity: Measuring Place Effects for Refugee Children
affiliations: University of Copenhagen, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Economics, Finance, Accounting (EFA), University of Copenhagen, University of Copenhagen and Rockwool Foundation Research Unit

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

affiliations.org_name: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Economics, Finance, Accounting (EFA)

detail.abstract: Area-level measures of economic opportunity are increasingly used to guide place-based policies. We study whether these measures predict long-run outcomes for a vulnerable population: over 12,000 refugee children quasi-randomly assigned to municipalities under Denmark's 1986–1998 dispersal policy. We focus on predetermined measures of opportunity available when children arrive and validate them using a mover-exposure design among permanent residents. Moving from a low- to a high-opportunity area (a two-standard-deviation increase) raises adult income rank by 3 percentile points (7.5 percent) and employment by 4 percentage points. It also reduces criminal convictions by 14 percent and teen parenthood by 19 percent, with more modest effects on educational attainment. Economic opportunity predicts crime and teen parenthood more strongly than other area characteristics, including local crime rates. For adult income, area-level inequality is a particularly strong predictor. These findings suggest that social mobility in the areas where refugee children grow up meaningfully shapes their long-term wellbeing.

detail.abstract: The United States has long lacked comprehensive household spending data across all types of households. Data sources whose primary purpose is to measure spending routinely miss the highest-income and wealthiest households (Bee, Meyer, and Sullivan, 2015; Sabelhaus, Johnson, Ash, Swanson, Garner, Greenlees, and Henderson, 2015; Pfeffer, Schoeni, Kennickell, and Andreski, 2016), while data sources that cover the full distribution of income and wealth lack comprehensive spending measures (Attanasio and Pistaferri, 2016; Fisher, Johnson, Smeeding, and Thompson, 2022).

title: Debiasing Law Enforcement Officers: Evidence from an Expressive Arts Intervention in India
affiliations: World Bank, World Bank, Northeastern University (USA) and Princeton University

detail.title: Debiasing Law Enforcement Officers: Evidence from an Expressive Arts Intervention in India

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Frontline state agents exercise substantial discretion over citizens’ access to public services, yet little is known about whether the attitudes and beliefs shaping this discretion can be changed among incumbent bureaucrats. Partnering with the Bihar Police - one of India’s largest states that operates under comparatively severe policing capacity constraints, we conduct a cluster randomized controlled trial across 417 police stations and roughly 2,500 active duty senior field police officers to evaluate a three-day expressive arts intervention, grounded in the Theatre of the Oppressed, designed to change police responses to gender-based violence (GBV). Approximately 7 months after baseline, treated officers exhibit more favorable attitudes toward GBV, greater empathy, and stronger legal knowledge. These changes translate into observed policing behavior: in standardized victim audits conducted one year later, officers in treated stations are 15 percentage points less likely to blame victims, dismiss fewer complaints, and provide more referrals, while administrative records show a 41 percent reduction in registration delays and, over a longer horizon, increased GBV reporting by citizens. Exploiting variation generated by officer transfers, we find suggestive evidence that these effects persist when treated officers relocate and diffuse to untreated officers working alongside treated colleagues. The effects also extend to the workplace: junior female officers working with treated senior officers report lower harassment and anxiety. These findings show that the attitudes shaping bureaucratic discretion are malleable and that changing how incumbent state agents exercise authority can improve both citizen-facing service delivery and the broader workplace environment.

detail.abstract: Informal support networks, the interpersonal connections through which families provide or receive financial and practical assistance, constitute a critical but often invisible component of the U.S. economy. These networks can serve many of the same functions as wealth: shaping key economic decisions around saving, spending, and labor supply and providing an important buffer against adverse shocks (McGarry 2016; Bergeot et al., 2025).

detail.abstract: When students can postpone an exam, a salient leisure event can change both whether they are evaluated and how well they perform. I study this using the day-level alignment between 172,050 final-exam opportunities for 4,053 university students and salient World Cup and Copa América matches, including all Uruguay matches and selected late-stage games, from 2003 to 2014. An exam held the day after one of these matches has 3.9 percentage points higher nonattendance, grades among exam takers that are 0.14 standard deviations lower, and a 6.3 percentage-point lower probability of passing the scheduled opportunity—about 10 percent relative to the control mean. The grade effect is concentrated at this one-day horizon and remains similar with student fixed effects and flexible calendar controls. Because students can skip an exam without justification and use a later opportunity, the setting distinguishes a participation response from performance conditional on participation, two margins that compulsory-exam settings cannot separate. The results show that short-lived leisure shocks affect academic outcomes not only through performance, but also by changing when students choose to be evaluated.

title: Geopolitical Tensions, Social Identity and the Fragmentation of the Global Economy
affiliations: Independent, University of Passau and University of Passau

detail.title: Geopolitical Tensions, Social Identity and the Fragmentation of the Global Economy

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Geopolitical tensions threaten to fragment the global economy into rival blocs. As a driver of this fragmentation, we propose a demand-side channel grounded in social identity theory: consumers value goods partly by the political and economic values embodied in their origin. We embed this in a trade model with two countries that are similar in terms of political values and one dissimilar country, with the US, the EU and China as our benchmark example. We show that a geopolitical shock raising the salience of political over economic values diverts trade toward the similar pair and can also make a previously unattractive standards-harmonization agreement between them mutually beneficial. A subsequent estrangement of the similar pair, through diverging political values or trade-war measures, can reverse both effects and push the world economy from two blocs toward three. We also apply the framework to an estrangement of the US from the EU and Canada. Both a US divergence in political values and trade-war measures divert trade toward the EU-Canada pair, but only the former can make a previously unattractive EU-Canada agreement mutually beneficial.

title: Environmental and Economic Potential of Community-based Strawberry Agritourism for Sustainable Tourism in the Sembalun Area, East Lombok
affiliations: Sekolah Tinggi Pariwisata Mataram, Sekolah Tinggi Pariwisata Mataram, Sekolah Tinggi Pariwisata Mataram, Sekolah Tinggi Pariwisata Mataram and Sekolah Tinggi Pariwisata Mataram

detail.title: Environmental and Economic Potential of Community-based Strawberry Agritourism for Sustainable Tourism in the Sembalun Area, East Lombok

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No Conflict of Interest between author
declarations.funderStatement: No External Funding

detail.abstract: Sembalun, a highland district at the foot of Mount Rinjani in East Lombok, has turned its smallholder strawberry plots into one of Lombok's most recognisable agritourism products. This working paper assesses the environmental and economic potential of community-based strawberry agritourism in Sembalun and asks under what conditions it can contribute to sustainable tourism. Using an integrative review of secondary datapeer-reviewed and national journal articles, official statistics, community-service reports by the authors, and recent regional news reports-we synthesise evidence along economic, environmental and socio-institutional dimensions. The economic evidence is strong: agritourism-linked activities account for roughly 30% of local household income, strawberry farming alone for about 79% of the agritourism-linked share, and a community-managed pick-your-own scheme has reportedly lifted the farm-gate price from about IDR 5,000 to IDR 30,000 per kg. The environmental evidence is more ambivalent. Highland climate and volcanic soils are the resource base, yet the same base is exposed to rainfall anomalies, post-2018-earthquake water scarcity, conversion of farmland to cafés and lodging, and production on continuously cropped plots. We argue that strawberry agritourism is sustainable only when it is governed as a community commons: plot rotation, collective caps on farmer entry, retention of land ownership by local households, water-saving technology and gender-responsive benefit sharing. The paper closes with an explicit statement of the limitations of a secondary-data design and an agenda for primary, mixed-method research.

title: Adjudicating Mechanistic Theories of Psychopathology by Automated Adversarial Collaboration: Coverage, Misspecification, Identifiability, and Heterogeneity
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania and Pepperdine University - Pepperdine University

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is no declaration of interest as this is completely a theoretical paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This is not a study with patients/participants.

detail.abstract: Closed-loop systems that combine language-model "theory agents", program synthesis, and information-theoretic experimental design promise to adjudicate between competing theories of cognition at scale. Such systems merge theory-driven and data-driven modelling: theories supply structure, synthesis and flexible learners supply realizations and ceilings. We argue that their evidential claims are only as strong as an under-examined layer, namely the map from a theory to the models that stand in for it. We give a formal treatment of this map in the setting of computational psychiatry. We show that (i) theory-level evidence depends on the synthesizer's coverage distribution, with a sharp characterization of when a verdict is coverage-robust; (ii) under misspecification, posterior conaurration and expected-informationgain design are blind to the absolute adequacy of the winning theory, but a theory-agnostic wildcard model yields a detectable inadequacy gap; (iii) theories can be observationally confounded on a design space, and enlarging that space with interventions monotonically reduces confounding; (iv) evidence remains valid under automated model revision only if revisions are predictable with respect to the data history; and (v) population-level mechanistic claims are ill-defined without a heterogeneity model, and pooled adjudication can favour a minority mechanism. Two small simulations illustrate the results, and we state falsifiable predictions for the automated-adjudication literature.

detail.abstract: The literature on fixed exchange-rate regimes has long recognized that pegs are inherently impermanent, and that the time until a peg is realigned or abandoned depends on observable macroeconomic fundamentals-reserve adequacy, real exchange-rate misalignment, fiscal discipline-as well as on structural and political factors that are harder to monitor systematically but that the duration-analysis literature has shown to matter, including terms-of-trade shocks and executive political transitions (Klein and Marion, 1997). This paper formalizes peg sustainability as a Cox (1972) proportional-hazards survival problem, in the same statistical tradition used to model corporate default under incomplete information (Obstfeld and Rogoff, 1995), and partitions the covariate vector into a monitored block (reserve coverage, real effective exchangerate misalignment, and the fiscal balance-the variables a central bank or an IMF Article IV mission routinely tracks) and a structural/shock block (terms-of-trade shocks, political transition intensity, and regional monetary-union contagion pressure-factors the duration literature flags as important but that are not part of routine peg-sustainability monitoring in every currency union). Motivated by the institutional history of the CFA franc zone, whose two monetary unions have maintained a fixed external peg since 1945 with a single 50% realignment in January 1994 (International Monetary Fund, 1994), we study the properties of this hazard-based framework under a fully specified, parametrically known data-generating process rather than fitting it to a real crosscountry panel, because no de-identified, spell-level dataset of peg durations with verified realignment timing and both covariate blocks was available to us for this study. Across 1,500 simulated 30-year peg spells, adding the structural/shock block raises the concordance index from 0.641 to 0.693 and is jointly significant against the monitored-only model (likelihoodratio χ 2 3 = 91.2, p < 10-16); the discrimination gain scales with the assumed strength of the structural signal, degrades gracefully rather than catastrophically as structural-data coverage becomes incomplete, and the maximum-likelihood estimator shows correct confidence-interval coverage down to samples of 100 peg-spells-a sample size on the order of what a real historical crosscountry panel of fixed-exchange-rate episodes could plausibly provide. We interpret these as necessary, not sufficient, conditions for using hazard-based peg-sustainability monitoring in practice, and set out explicitly what an empirical study using a real historical panel of exchange-rate regimes would still need to show.

detail.abstract: Voluntary health-insurance studies often treat an affirmative response to a willingness-to-pay question as evidence of monetary demand. We examine whether that interpretation is valid using programme-evaluation data from SAJIDA Foundation's Smart Healthcare Service in Sunamganj, Bangladesh. Final treatment households were linked to prospective baseline records and compared with controls using overlap weighting based on pre-intervention health need, healthcare use and medical expenditure. The primary analytic sample contained 167 treatment and 103 control households; all primary balancing covariates had post-weighting absolute standardized mean differences below 0.10. At endline, 65.4% of treatment households expressed interest in paying for insurance compared with 94.8% of weighted controls (adjusted difference-29.4 percentage points; p<0.001). Yet 46 of 98 interested controls (46.9%) subsequently stated an annual contribution of BDT 0. When willingness to pay was defined as a strictly positive monetary amount, the weighted proportions were 65.4% for treatment and 50.3% for controls (difference +15.0 percentage points; p=0.074). Among respondents with positive WTP, mean annual amounts were BDT 772 and BDT 612, respectively (p=0.279). A broader demographic and socioeconomic sensitivity model produced the same qualitative pattern, although with smaller effective sample sizes and residual imbalance. Among treatment households, recent hospitalization was more common among those with positive WTP than among those without it (49.4% versus 32.5%; p=0.014). The results show that general interest, positive monetary commitment and contribution amount are distinct constructs. Binary interest questions may substantially overstate effective demand for unfamiliar insurance products. For programmes introducing unfamiliar insurance products, WTP elicitation should therefore follow a clear, standardized explanation of the insurance mechanism and the product's price, benefits and limitations.

detail.abstract: This paper explores the effect of export restrictions on critical minerals on foreign investment in exploration, the upstream activity that determines the future resource base. Using a three-way panel of countries, minerals and years that combines the OECD inventory of export restrictions on critical raw materials with S&P Global exploration budgets over the period 2009 to 2024, and a local-projections difference-in-differences estimator that accommodates the staggered adoption of restrictions, we find that the introduction of an export restriction has a statistically and economically significant negative effect on foreign exploration investment: about US$11 million (constant dollars) per country-mineral pair per year, or roughly 9% of the cost of exploring and developing a typical gold project. The effect is asymmetric, as removing a restriction does not restore investment. Outright export bans drive the result, whereas export taxes and quotas have no discernible effect on foreign exploration. The key results are driven by countries with weaker control of corruption, suggesting that the signalling effect of trade restrictions is pervasive when there is poor policy credibility. Finally, we verify that restrictions bind in practice: export values fall by about 15% after a restriction is introduced, with the largest declines for bans and quotas.

detail.abstract: Independent monetary policy institutions that keep inflation and unemployment in check arose from overlapping economic crises in the 1970s. But following the global financial crisis of 2008, at least a dozen political leaders successfully weakened central banks, tapping into mistrust in elites and experts. Only three years later, global democracy peaked, ushering in the present era of democratic erosion. Despite the apparent intersection of these two shifts, few studies explore connections between them. This is surprising since research links central bank independence (CBI) to democratic quality, and autocrats see monetary manipulation as a device to mitigate fiscal irresponsibility. In this essay we argue that CBI offers a compelling litmus test for whether countries submit to or resist democratic decay. Our theory suggests that by the time executives politicize central banks, they have already taken other illiberal steps such as undermining media freedom, stoking polarization, or undermining civil society independence. Our literature review summarizes evidence regarding the benefits of CBI and situates dedelegation of monetary authority within the autocrat's repertoire. Statistical tests first demonstrate a strong correlation between CBI and democracy. Second, this relationship largely disappears in dynamic models-expect where we use a break point to cluster the years after democracy peaked. This strongly suggests that central banks demonstrate some resilience in the face of democratic erosion. Third, models disaggregating democracy find mixed relationships with variables measuring attacks on media freedom and political polarization, hallmarks of erosion. But there is a strong and consistent relationship with civil society freedom, which we interpret as reinforcing the ability (and willingness) of firms and voters to protect central banks' efforts to manage inflation. The results hold across a range of economic controls, as well as a proxy for majoritarian democracy. Our conclusion discusses how these findings advance our understanding of democratic erosion, by placing recent attacks on central bankers within our understanding of the political business cycle.

detail.abstract: The new view of dividend taxation bundles three logically distinct claims: capitalisation, that a permanent dividend tax is impounded in share values; the Auerbach prediction, that the firm's real retention and investment decision is unchanged; and the King criterion, that the tax does not enter the cost of capital. In a frictionless two-period general-equilibrium economy with an all-equity firm and a power production technology, we show that the three claims hold under progressively stronger conditions. Capitalisation always holds, since the tax cancels from the firm's investment first-order condition, and in partial equilibrium Fisher separation delivers the new view in full. The failures are general-equilibrium phenomena that sort by margin: a subsistence level of consumption in otherwise standard HARA preferences breaks the Auerbach prediction for any technology, whereas the King criterion fails only when returns to capital are also decreasing, with a magnitude proportional to the product of technological curvature and the subsistence level. These breaks are uncompensated income effects, not substitution distortions: a revenue-neutral lump-sum rebate restores neutrality for any preferences and any technology. No friction is needed, only the curvature of preferences and technology and the breakdown of Fisher separation when the firm is the sole store of value. The all-equity assumption is inessential; under risk, by contrast, an asymmetric loss offset distorts the price of risk, a substitution distortion that no lump-sum rebate can repair.

detail.abstract: The center of main interests (COMI) is an organizing principle and one of the central pillars of the Model Law on Cross-Border Insolvency enacted by the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL) and adopted by more than 60 jurisdictions around the world. By incentivizing the initiation of insolvency proceedings in the debtor's economic "center of gravity" under the threat that proceedings commenced elsewhere may not be recognized, or at least not as foreign main proceedings, COMI seeks to promote predictability and the fair and efficient administration of cross-border insolvencies while limiting forum shopping. Relative to these goals, we show, COMI is a failure. Litigation is common because a firm's COMI is often unclear; forum shopping is rampant, with large corporations viewing COMI as simply a tax that must be paid to local creditors; and the fair and efficient administration of cross-border insolvencies is stymied by COMI, which prevents medium-sized enterprises from selecting the insolvency system that can best maximize creditor recoveries. The trouble with COMI, we argue, is that it confuses value maximization with distributional fairness. Fairness may require honoring the priority rules of the debtor's COMI, but value maximization may require the use of a more efficient insolvency system. We show how to fix this problem.

detail.abstract: How much of the defense premium that appears around geopolitical shocks reflects exposure to defense contracts, and how much reflects the fact that defense contractors are low beta? I study six events in the 2025–2026 Iran Conflict using 70 U.S.-listed firms over 491 trading days, of which 47 have defense contract revenue and 23 have none. Defense exposure is measured from Federal procurement records. The paper reports two results. The substantive one is a sign reversal: the cross-sectional correlation between defense exposure and same-day abnormal returns is +0.53 on 13 June 2025, when Israel struck Iran, and-0.51 on 24 June 2025, when the United States struck and a ceasefire was announced; the difference is significant under a paired bootstrap over firms (p < 0.001) and is not matched by any other eleven-day pair in the sample (randomization inference p = 0.081). Read as a group difference, firms with defense contracts outperformed firms with none by +1.78 percentage points on 13 June and underperformed them by 2.08 points on 24 June; roughly a third of that spread reflects the fact that defense contractors are low-beta and technology firms are high-beta, and after adjusting for each firm's own beta the spread narrows to +1.13 and-1.44 points while remaining significant. A formal result underlies the decomposition. Because the market return is common to all firms on a given day, subtracting it is a location shift and leaves every cross-sectional statistic exactly unchanged: firm-level market adjustment cannot remove market-wide variation from a cross sectional event study, and the adjustment must be firm-specific to do so. The methodological finding is that this is nearly all that survives. None of the four event-window mean abnormal returns is statistically significant, and the largest of them, +0.66% on 13 June (t = 1.81), has a randomization-inference p-value of 0.62: days producing cross-sectional averages that large are common. The two approaches disagree because they treat different units as the sample — firms or days — and the treatment in an event study varies at the level of the day. Across a family of 29 reported tests, false-discovery-rate control leaves three results standing at 5%. The paper's contribution is as much the demonstration as the finding: in a small event study, the choice of sampling unit determines whether a result exists.

detail.abstract: Can complex machine-learning models forecast publicly reported bank risk ratios more reliably than a simple rule that keeps the latest value unchanged? We study 12 institutions in Mozambique using 32 quarterly prudential reports for 2018–2025. The audited analytic panel contains 362 bank-quarter records and 349 valid consecutive-quarter forecasting pairs. We compare persistence, observed-variable path regressions, ridge regression, random forest and a regression-plus-random-forest hybrid. Of these pairs, 253 have target dates through 2023; the other 96 cover 2024–2025, a period previously examined during exploratory model development. The proposed two-factor latent structural equation model fails measurement checks (CFI = 0.519; RMSEA = 0.248; SRMR = 0.160). For the 96 retrospective evaluation pairs, persistence achieves the lowest mean absolute error for both non-performing loans (0.0339) and liquid assets (0.0556). Random forest achieves liquidity RMSE of 0.0884, nearly equal to persistence (0.0883), but is less accurate for non-performing loans. Rare, large changes and the small number of banks limit the conclusions. The study offers a source-audited and executable assessment of when extra predictive complexity does not add reliable value under public-data constraints.

detail.abstract: Geopolitical fragmentation is reshaping how multinational enterprises (MNEs) organize and manage international business networks. Although recent research has examined how firms respond to geopolitical uncertainty through resilience building and network reconfiguration, less is understood about how adaptation unfolds across heterogeneous international business relationships. This study develops a relationship-centered perspective of geopolitical adaptation by introducing the concept of Selective Network Adaptation. We argue that MNEs do not uniformly restructure their international networks in response to geopolitical fragmentation; instead, they selectively adjust different relationships according to their strategic importance, political exposure, technological dependence, and adjustment costs. Using China firm panel data from multinational enterprises, we find that geopolitical exposure generates asymmetric network adaptation. Firms actively adjust customer relationships, whereas supplier relationships remain comparatively stable. Further analyses reveal why firms facing similar geopolitical pressures adopt different adaptation patterns by highlighting the roles of political constraints, technological characteristics, and organizational capability. This study contributes to research on geopolitical strategy and international business networks by showing that geopolitical adaptation is not a uniform firm-level response but a relationship-centered organizational process. The concept of Selective Network Adaptation explains why MNEs facing similar geopolitical pressures may reorganize their international networks in different ways.

detail.abstract: In H1 2026, cryptocurrency market continued its downward trend. detail.abstract: The national financial accounts record who owes a claim and who holds it, never which income pays it. This paper adds that dimension. Labor backing accounts decompose United States financial claims twice over, by the income attributed to servicing each and by who holds, guarantees or owes it, across thirteen claim classes from 1947 to 2025. No source observes which income funds a payment, so we observe the income composition of the parties owing each class and attribute in proportion: every figure here is an attribution under that convention, not measured servicing. About 52 percent of US debt, public and private, is attributed to labor income on the direct route, and 60 percent once the indirect route is counted. Counting the federal government as exposed when it is holder, guarantor or debtor, it stands behind about 79.5 percent of directly wage-attributed claims, against 1 percent of the separately measured claims on AI capital. That share is a return rather than new, tracing a U from 70 percent in 1947. Claims are spread far more evenly than the income attributed to servicing them: the index of claim share to wage-bill share falls from 1.41 in the second quintile to 0.65 at the top, or 2.10 and 0.97 claims per wage dollar on the level basis. We state every convention, move each at a time, and report a pre-registered test in which the measure fails to predict bank credit losses. These are accounts, not a risk measure.

detail.abstract: News-jump regressions are high-frequency event-study regressions under infill asymptotics. When news-jumps in explanatory variables over narrow observation windows are of the same magnitude as diffusive background noise, the regression coefficient is weakly identified, invalidating least-squares estimation and inference. We develop identification-robust inference based on Anderson-Rubin tests and derive, in a Gaussian limit experiment arising from the jump-diffusion process, a minimal sufficient and complete statistic for jumps, thereby enabling powerful conditional inference. In applications to FOMC announcements, we invert the tests to study the Fed information effect of Nakamura and Steinsson (2018) at one-minute frequency, and to examine market-factor dependence in news-driven ETF jumps.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how remote work reshapes wage anchoring inside firms. In settings where productivity is imperfectly observed and tasks are heterogenous, firms have traditionally tied pay to local industry benchmarks. We develop a wage-setting framework in which compensation combines a firm's assessment of worker productivity with an external benchmark, and show that remote work weakens anchoring through two reinforcing forces: labor market integration, which broadens recruiting beyond local markets, raises the level and dispersion of outside options, and diminishes the salience of a single local benchmark; and information frictions, as distributed collaboration changes the quality of performance signals and prompts adjustments in evaluation and compensation governance. Using online job postings from major Chinese recruitment platforms matched to listed firms from 2014 to 2024, we construct firm-year measures of remote work adoption and find that higher remote work intensity corresponds to larger deviations of firm-level labor costs from industry benchmark wages. A directional decomposition shows the effect is driven primarily by above-benchmark premia, consistent with recruiting specialized, digitally complementary talent and paying compensating differentials, rather than by below-benchmark discounts. The relationship is stronger in firms with greater digital capabilities, higher innovation intensity, and more complex organizations, and is most pronounced early in diffusion before partial re-anchoring. Effects are larger among state-owned enterprises, and among large, eastern, and manufacturing firms. Overall, digital labor market integration weakens wage anchoring, shifts pay toward organization-and match-specific determinants, and widens cross-firm disparities.

detail.abstract: Institutions rarely decide, in a single act, that something should be forgotten, left uninvestigated or disbelieved. They decide it through a sequence of small, defensible steps: a record is classified, a request is answered with "not located," an account finds no corroboration, a subject loses priority, a source acquires a reputation for unseriousness, and the resulting absence is finally read as proof of irrelevance. This article names that sequence cascade selectivity and defines it as the operation of successive, interdependent filters kept by different institutions, in which the output of each filter conditions the input of the next. It distinguishes the category from censorship, formal secrecy, conspiracy, informational cascades, the Matthew effect and epistemic injustice; describes six filters (classification, access and custody, corroboration, prioritization, credibility and recognition); and proposes a minimal, falsifiable model with a dependence coefficient and a logarithmic index. Using Brazilian law as the principal setting (Constitution arts. 5, XXXIII and XXXV, 37 and 216; Law 12,527/2011; Law 8,159/1991), it argues that the law regulates the first filter densely and the downstream filters thinly, leaving the "not located" answer without verifiable procedure. A limit case concerning archival custody and a judicial access request on Brazil's 1977 Operation Prato is analyzed strictly as an institutional object, without any claim about the phenomena reported. Comparative material from the United States, the United Kingdom and the Inter-American system, and the article's explicit falsification conditions, frame its doctrinal implications.

detail.abstract: This study examines how much a Pairgap-style co-buying model could reduce up-front monetary barriers for small individual investors compared with traditional solo ownership in New York City. In high-cost urban New York City boroughs, standard down payments and transaction costs can create substantial entry barriers that require over a decade of continuous household savings, as can be seen in this model. A deterministic, scenario-based financial simulation integrated county-level Zillow Home Value Index valuations with U.S. Census median household incomes across all five boroughs. Evaluating two- and three-person cohorts across symmetrical and asymmetrical equity splits revealed that co-buying cuts individual upfront cash hurdles and savings timelines by roughly one-half to four-fifths (49.7% to 79.7%). Upfront capital dropped from $163,027 to $49,178 for a 30% share in Manhattan, and to $13,249 for a 20% share in the Bronx, compressing savings timelines from nearly 16 years to approximately 3.2 years. While collaborative purchasing effectively lowers monetary entry barriers via proportional equity fractionalization, it does not discount underlying property values. Consequently, investors exchange upfront cash hurdles for non-monetary trade-offs, including shared mortgage liability, multi-party governance, and reduced liquidity (Koch et al., 2024).

detail.abstract: Neoclassical frameworks frequently conceptualize demand as a static parameter, confining extreme behavioral deviations to highly specific environments. This paper explores an alternative paradigm, modeling demand as a dynamic, state-dependent phenomenon for necessities lacking close substitutes. Commodities generally exhibit negatively sloping demand curves under normal market conditions. Evidence suggests, however, that severe exogenous price and supply shocks may induce profound regime changes. Drawing upon threshold models of expectations, the proposed framework hypothesizes that market behavior operates in a conventional downward-sloping mode until a supply disruption exceeds a specific perception boundary. Once this boundary is breached, the market transitions into a crisis state. In this environment, expectations regarding future scarcity appear to trigger a divergent shift in purchasing behavior, motivating institutional actors to rationally pre-pone procurement. Anticipating stockouts, actors abandon traditional consumption smoothing to hoard available supply, precipitating an aggressive outward shift in the demand curve. This state-dependent displacement, while empirically mimicking perfect inelasticity, manifests strictly as a short-run temporal anomaly, with aggregate long-run demand remaining downwardsloping. The resulting theoretical model details how baseline price sensitivity breaks down under severe duress. We empirically test this framework using high-frequency European energy market data from January 2018 through August 2026. By incorporating continuous controls for institutional storage mandates and instrumenting for price endogeneity through a cross-validated two-stage least squares approach, we attempt to reconcile institutional procurement behavior with macroeconomic outcomes. Allowing the data to endogenously determine the threshold via an instrumented grid search reveals a statistically significant regime shift where accumulation driven by scarcity heavily offsets standard price elasticity. While broad aggregations present inherent ecological limitations, these findings offer preliminary support for state-dependent hoarding phenomena in wholesale commodity markets.

detail.abstract: Losses and damages from the impacts of climate change are already reshaping economic development pathways. However, so too are mitigation and adaptation actions taken in response to climate change. As countries implement climate policies with increasing ambition and scale, cross-border effects arise for other countries. Building on evolving conceptualisations of transboundary climate risk we set out a framework to map policy measures, transboundary flow alterations and transmission mechanisms that give rise to international risks and opportunities. Drawing empirically from observable effects across five Low-and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs), we identify that climate-related responses in other countries across domains such as energy, industrial, migration and defence policy, can transmit effects through a range of flows (trade, finance, people, biophysical, technology) and mechanisms (prices, production factors, norms, security). Failure to adequately conceptualise how climate responses in one country will affect others, the transmission pathways and channels to respond, has major implications for the current fragile consensus on addressing the climate emergency. New conceptual frameworks to enhance understanding of the channels of impact will better equip policymakers and researchers to anticipate the full spectrum of cross-border spillovers, manage risks governance, and identify opportunities.

title: Sustainable Agriculture: A Necessity, not a Privilege? Productivity, Nitrogen and Growth in 75 Developing Countries, 1971–2023, with Evidence from Bangladesh
affiliations: The University of Manchester

detail.title: Sustainable Agriculture: A Necessity, not a Privilege? Productivity, Nitrogen and Growth in 75 Developing Countries, 1971–2023, with Evidence from Bangladesh

detail.abstract: Does it matter how a developing country's agriculture grows, by using more inputs or by using them better? This paper combines the USDA's decomposition of agricultural growth into total factor productivity and four inputs with FAO nitrogen balances and UN national accounts in a gap-free panel of 102 countries for 1971–2023, 75 of them low- or middle-income, and tests hypotheses written down before estimation. In the typical developing country, inputs supplied three-quarters of output growth. Over five-year periods, growth in fertiliser and feed is accompanied by a rising nitrogen surplus, whereas productivity growth is accompanied by rising nitrogen use efficiency, a larger fall in emissions per unit of output and an unchanged surplus; these associations are contemporaneous, partly a matter of accounting and partly reversed in the next period. A higher surplus is associated with faster later productivity growth only below about 15 kg N/ha. Across developing countries the surplus rises with income and turns down only among high-income countries, yet eleven of 29 developing countries with a substantial surplus reduced it after 2000 while raising output, regardless of income and without slower growth. Two hypotheses are not supported: a decade of productivity-led growth is not followed by faster non-farm growth than input-led growth, and greater exposure to world urea prices does not predict larger output losses. In Bangladesh the surplus rose from 138 to 169 kg N/ha while Vietnam's fell; whether Bangladesh's productivity growth has turned negative depends on an undocumented choice of cost shares in the published accounts.

title: Techno- economic analysis and Development Renewable Energy Installation Model on Telecommunication Industry in Zambia a case of Lusaka and Eastern Regions
affiliations: The university of Zambia, The university of Zambia and The university of Zambia

detail.title: Techno- economic analysis and Development Renewable Energy Installation Model on Telecommunication Industry in Zambia a case of Lusaka and Eastern Regions
detail.abstract:
The telecommunication industry in Zambia which stands out as a linchpin to social-economic
development is undergoing rapid transformation driven by technological advancements, increasing
user demand, and the deployment of next-generation networks such as 4G, Massive MIMO, and
non-standalone 5G. However, the greatest challenge is energy sustainability to keep the network
running as the industry mainly relies on unstable grid and expensive fossil fuel. In selected cases,
telecom companies have tried to install solar PVs for powering off grid sites. However,
installations have been done poorly due to lack of installation models.
This study presents a techno-economic analysis and development of Renewable Energy
Installation Model (REIM) for telecommunication infrastructure in Zambia, using selected sites in
Lusaka and Eastern Provinces as case studies. The study integrates Geographic information
Systems (GIS), Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA), HOMER Pro optimization, and PVsyst
simulation tools to assess renewable energy resource potential and identify optimal energy
configurations for the telecommunication sites. Primary data was obtained from
telecommunication operators, tower companies, and site surveys, while secondary data were
obtained from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), National Renewable
Energy Laboratory (NREL), metrological databases, and published literature.
The findings reveal that solar photovoltaic systems combined with lithium-ion battery backup
constitute the most technologically feasible, economically viable, and environmentally sustainable
solution for telecommunication infrastructure across the study regions. Simulation results indicate
that well-sized solar- battery systems can achieve a renewable energy fraction approaching 100%,
eliminate diesel dependency, significantly reduce operational expenditure, and minimize carbon
emissions. Furthermore, the study establishes a predictive relationship between site load and
photovoltaic capacity requirements, resulting in the development of a region-specific installation
model for the telecommunications infrastructure.
The practical applicability of the proposed model was validated through implementation at
Nansenga Repeater station and IHS Zambia Headquarters, where significant reductions in fossil
fuel consumption and operational costs where achieved. The study contributes to the body of
knowledge by providing a standardized renewable energy installation framework for
telecommunications infrastructure and a replicable methodology for sustainable energy planning
in developing countries.

title: Investing in Your Enemies?
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR)

detail.abstract: International diversification can expose investors to issuers whose strategic interests may become adverse to their own, creating risks not captured by conventional portfolio analysis. This paper distinguishes geopolitical harm from financial losses on foreign claims and develops a stylized portfolio model incorporating conflict-related impairment, issuer political alignment, institutional trust, and benchmark discipline. The model shows that higher conflict risk, stronger adversarial alignment, and weaker institutional trust reduce optimal foreign exposure, while benchmark sensitivity sustains holdings even when investors internalize geopolitical harm. This explains how benchmark inclusion can recast substantive geopolitical allocations as neutral implementation decisions. The analysis further shows that formal issuer type is an inadequate guide: politically aligned corporations may reinforce hostile state capacity much like sovereign borrowers. Strategic asset allocation and benchmark design should consider geopolitical alignment, legal enforceability, transferability, and convertibility when assessing foreign investments.

detail.abstract: This paper estimates what a marginal dollar of cash was worth to the shareholders of 5,173 United States non-financial firms over 2006–2022, and whose cash was worth more, using Faulkender–Wang return regressions on 39,445 firm-years that include firms later delisted. A dollar is worth 1.29 dollars at the sample means. With firm characteristics measured before the year's return, cash is worth more at firms that made a loss in the previous year, lack an investment-grade rating, are recently listed or have high Tobin's q, and less at the smallest firms and at firms whose debt is mostly short-term; the Kaplan–Zingales, Whited–Wu and size–age indices carry no reliable information. End-of-year sorting produces two further results that vanish under start-of-year sorting. An apparent premium on cash held through funding stress comes from the single recovery year 2009; stress has no reliable effect. The loss and size results depend on the return benchmark.

title: The End of the 1981–2021 Monetary Supercycle
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The End of the 1981–2021 Monetary Supercycle

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known financial or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that the period from approximately 1981 through 2021 constituted a monetary supercycle in which declining interest rates, structural forces that restrained inflation, globalization, expanding financial markets and increasingly powerful central-bank intervention allowed debt and financial claims to grow while their long-term financing cost continued to fall. The pandemic response of 2020 marked the culmination of many of those forces; by 2022, persistent inflation and the break above the long-term declining interest-rate channel signaled a materially different financial environment. The paper uses historical comparisons to place the current transition in a broader historical context. Britain after the Napoleonic Wars and John Law's France provide contrasting examples of how economies confronted large inherited financial burdens, while gold and silver reserves under the Bretton Woods-era system and the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve illustrate how accumulated reserves can delay adjustment after underlying conditions begin to change. Japan is treated as an extreme contemporary example worth monitoring as events unfold, as its position within global financial markets could make it an important lynchpin in the current transition. The central argument is that the emerging environment may be increasingly constrained by higher financing costs and the erosion of the structural tailwinds that supported the previous monetary regime, while faster growth in productive capacity and real output could relieve those pressures by expanding the economic base faster than debt and financial claims accumulate. Artificial intelligence, robotics and other productivity-enhancing investments could provide a path through these constraints, but only if today's capital spending translates into greater productive capacity, higher productivity and sustained growth in real output.

title: Investment Stimulus, Automation, and Skill Demand
affiliations: Sungkyunkwan University and Bank of Korea

detail.title: Investment Stimulus, Automation, and Skill Demand
detail.abstract:
This paper studies how a policy-driven reduction in the cost of capital affects firm-level
labor demand and its skill composition. Using the expansion of bonus depreciation in
the 2017 U.S. tax reform as an exogenous variation in capital costs, we find that firms
facing larger cost reductions raise capital expenditure on machinery and equipment
while lowering employment and job postings. Using detailed information on skill re-
quirements and patents at the firm level, we show that the decline in labor demand is
concentrated in job positions requiring few software skills and in firms holding more
robot-related patents, a pattern suggestive of automation as a potential mechanism.
Interpreting the reduced-form estimates through a task-based model, we estimate that
the elasticity of substitution between capital and labor varies substantially across firms
and job positions.

title: Sulfuric Acid Roasting and Water Leaching for Efficient Lithium Extraction from Clay-type Ores
affiliations: Zhengzhou University, Zhengzhou University, Zhengzhou University, Zhengzhou University and Zhengzhou University

detail.title: Sulfuric Acid Roasting and Water Leaching for Efficient Lithium Extraction from Clay-type Ores
detail.abstract:
Clay-type lithium ores are important but technologically challenging
resources, mainly attributed to the refractory nature of lithium-bearing minerals. This
study proposes a concentrated sulfuric acid roasting combined with water leaching
process that achieves 92.01% lithium extraction under optimized conditions of
roasting 60 min at 250℃ with an acid-to-ore of 0.45 mL/g, and water leaching 60 min
at 80℃ with a liquid-to-solid ratio of 4 mL/g. XRD and FTIR analyses show that the
roasting process effectively decomposes the silicate structures such as illite and
montmorillonite, and transforms the refractory lithium-bearing silicates into readily
soluble sulfates, enabling the efficient release of lithium into the leachate. This offers
a low-temperature and energy-conscious alternative for the economic extraction of
clay-type lithium reserves.

title: Distributed Convolutional Rank Regression over Decentralized Networks

detail.title: Distributed Convolutional Rank Regression over Decentralized Networks

affiliations.org_name: Changchun University of Science and Technology

detail.abstract: This paper studies convolution rank regression (CRR) over decentralized distributed learning networks. We propose a novel decentralized CRR framework, in which estimators are obtained by solving consensus-constrained optimization with kernel-smoothed rank loss. The developed estimation scheme relies solely on local node data and information shared by neighboring nodes, thereby achieving privacy preservation and high communication efficiency. For heterogeneous network settings, we establish finite-sample error bounds for the decentralized CRR estimator and derive exact support recovery guarantees for the sparse decentralized CRR Lasso estimator. To facilitate numerical implementation, we adopt a generalized consensus ADMM to efficiently solve local subproblems across all network nodes. We verify the favorable performance of our developed approach via extensive numerical simulations and real-data experiments.

title: Buying Duration: Index Rebalancing and Price Pressure in Government Bond Markets
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Department of Business Economics, Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) and Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR)

detail.title: Buying Duration: Index Rebalancing and Price Pressure in Government Bond Markets

declarations.funderStatement: Erasmus University Rotterdam

detail.abstract: Major fixed-income indices rebalance at month-end, systematically increasing index duration. We show that the resulting demand for duration generates predictable price pressure in highly liquid government bond markets. Duration-scaled government bond futures earn 1.19 basis points on the last trading day, versus 0.07 basis points on other days, with month-ends accounting for 47% of average monthly returns. The effect peaks around the index pricing snapshot, partially reverses afterward, strengthens with larger duration extensions and higher interest-rate volatility, and shifts after Bloomberg changed its index pricing time. Our results show that benchmark-constrained investors generate non-informational price pressure in liquid government bond markets.

title: Synchronous Structural Change and the Spatial Micro-foundations of Economic Transformation in Sub-Saharan Africa
affiliations: Wuhan University and Wuhan University

detail.title: Synchronous Structural Change and the Spatial Micro-foundations of Economic Transformation in Sub-Saharan Africa
detail.abstract: Sustained growth in Sub-Saharan Africa requires moving beyond isolated sectoral shifts toward synchronized structural change. Because macroeconomic reallocations do not occur in a geographic vacuum, analyzing their efficacy necessitates an integrated spatial framework. This study investigates the joint impact of synchronous structural change and subnational spatial configurations on regional economic transformation, uncovering non-linear cluster thresholds and micro-founded entrepreneurial transmission channels. We deploy dynamic System GMM, IV-2SLS, and recursive mediation specifications to isolate the direct, conditional, and mediated pathways connecting structural change, manufacturing clusters, and firm entry to macroeconomic transformation outcomes. The empirical results demonstrate that synchronous structural change exerts a robust positive direct effect on economic transformation. Crucially, this relationship is non-linearly moderated by manufacturing cluster density, revealing a critical localized threshold beyond which agglomeration economies amplify growth returns. Furthermore, recursive mediation analysis establishes that opportunity-driven entrepreneurial density serves as the primary micro-transmission mechanism, whereas survivalist self-employment exhibits zero transformative capacity. Regional development strategies must therefore transition away from monocentric urban pooling toward secondary polycentric manufacturing clusters while systematically supporting opportunity-driven entrepreneurs to mitigate localized crowding-out effects.

title: Which Dimension of External Financial Flows Promotes Environmental Sustainability in Africa: The Role of Institutional Quality
affiliations: University of South Africa and University of South Africa

detail.title: Which Dimension of External Financial Flows Promotes Environmental Sustainability in Africa: The Role of Institutional Quality
detail.abstract: With the growing reliance of African economies on external financial flows to support development, concerns remain over whether these inflows improve or worsen environmental sustainability. However, the environmental effects of different financing channels and the role of institutional quality remain unclear. To address this issue, we employ the Pooled Mean Group (PMG) estimator in an Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) panel for eight African economies to assess the effects of foreign direct investment, official development assistance and remittances on CO₂ emissions. Our findings show that foreign direct investment reduces emissions in the long run, while remittances and official development assistance increase environmental pressure. Institutional quality moderates these effects differently, reducing the emission effect of remittances but reinforcing that of foreign direct investment. These findings suggest that the environmental value of external finance depends on both the type of financial inflow and the institutional conditions under which it is utilised.

title: Can Inflation in Nigeria’s Land-border Neighbours Improve Short-term Inflation Forecasts? Out-of-Sample Evidence
affiliations: Central Bank of Nigeria, Central Bank of Nigeria, Central Bank of Nigeria and Central Bank of Nigeria

detail.title: Can Inflation in Nigeria’s Land-border Neighbours Improve Short-term Inflation Forecasts? Out-of-Sample Evidence
detail.abstract: This paper asks whether inflation in Nigeria’s four land-border neighbours (Niger, Benin, Chad and Cameroon) helps to forecast Nigerian headline inflation. Using monthly data for January 2011–February 2026, we estimate direct multi-step forecasting regressions by ordinary least squares on an expanding window, using only observations dated before each forecast origin under an assumed one-month publication lag. Forecasts 1, 3, 6 and 12 months ahead are evaluated over January 2019–December 2024 by root mean squared error (RMSE), with the Clark–West test for nested models and the Diebold–Mariano test with the Harvey–Leybourne–Newbold correction for non-nested models. At the one-month horizon, adding the neighbours to a benchmark with Nigeria’s own inflation and global food and oil prices lowers the RMSE from 0.999 to 0.965 percentage points, a 3.4 per cent gain that is significant at the 1 per cent level. The gain remains significant at the 5 per cent level when the naira exchange rate is added. The border model is significantly more accurate than a model with four non-border African economies, and more accurate, though not significantly, than a model with four non-border CFA-franc economies. The gain is sensitive to the estimation start date: it disappears when estimation starts in July 2014. Because the petrol-price series begins then, the role of petrol cannot be assessed. The gain also disappears if the neighbours’ data are assumed to arrive three months late. Neighbouring inflation is therefore a candidate supplementary indicator for short-term monitoring. The results concern forecasting, not cross-border causation.

detail.abstract: In this paper, we show that gender gaps in performance on high-stakes exams, relative to lower-stakes assessments, are partly shaped by exam-preparation environments. Using rich data from French elite STEM programs, we document a gender gap in admissions to the most selective graduate schools. Quasi-experimental evidence shows this gap is larger among students preparing for exams in more selective tracks, with point estimates indicating disproportionate gains among men rather than underperformance by women. Cross-cohort variation points to fewer female peers and women's weaker response to high-ability male peers as partial explanations. These findings help explain women's underrepresentation in elite programs and the gender pay gap among top STEM workers.

title: Beyond Recognition: Judicial Specification of Climate and Biodiversity Duties in Environmental Constitutionalism

detail.title: Beyond Recognition: Judicial Specification of Climate and Biodiversity Duties in Environmental Constitutionalism

detail.abstract: Constitutions and courts in several regions now recognize some form of environmental right in the climate context, yet the decisions that have most visibly altered state conduct are not distinguished by the textual form of the right invoked. This article asks how adjudicators convert constitutional and rights-based environmental protection into enforceable climate and biodiversity obligations, and whether the availability of that conversion explains more of the variation in outcomes than the framing of the right. Using doctrinal and comparative legal analysis, it examines a purposive set of decisions and advisory opinions from Germany, the Netherlands, South Korea, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Montana, the European Court of Human Rights, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea and the International Court of Justice. The existing literature documents the spread of constitutional environmental provisions and a "rights turn" in climate litigation, but gives comparatively little systematic attention to the remedial content that follows recognition. The article advances a central thesis: the practical force of environmental constitutionalism depends less on whether a right is explicit, implicit, intertemporal or nature-centred than on whether a court can require political institutions to specify obligations in determinate, time-indexed and reviewable form, anchored to benchmarks the state has itself accepted. Biodiversity adjudication remains comparatively site-specific, a pattern attributed tentatively to the absence of a quantitative benchmark equivalent to a carbon budget. The strongest objection, that specification exceeds judicial competence and that no agreed fair-share metric exists, is assessed, and the thesis is qualified accordingly. The article closes with implications for judicial practice and constitutional design and states the conditions under which its thesis would fail. The analysis is doctrinal and makes no empirical claim about emissions outcomes.

detail.abstract: Declining birth cohorts leave schools and housing underused, so immigrant placement matters. We study Sweden's 2015 asylum placements, which needed no municipal consent. Within counties, among low-fertility municipalities, one additional asylum seeker per 100 residents lowered the share of small schools closed by 2017 from 20 to about 15 percent; two-thirds of averted closures persisted through 2024. Native births rose among resident women. A calibrated model of fertility, schools, and placement sends refugees where seats and housing are spare, gaining SEK 200,000 ($20,000) per refugee over Sweden's 2016 allocation. Spare capacity also raises the optimal intake.

detail.abstract:
The article is devoted to the development of a methodology for ensuring sustainable economic development of the enterprise, which calls for the solution of the theoretical basis of the resource management potential management process in the context of improving the concept of "resource potential of the enterprise".
In modern economic conditions, the mechanism of managing the resource potential of enterprises does not fully meet the objectives of increasing the efficiency of work and further development, which negatively affects the final results of enterprises, meeting the needs of consumers agricultural products and ensuring the level of food security of the country. Ensuring effective development of the domestic agrarian sector and the production of high-quality competitive agricultural products requires changes, first of all, regarding the organization of the use of the resource potential, as well as ensuring the implementation of innovative and resource-saving production technologies. Based on the results of deterministic factor analysis, we can now formulate the priorities of modernizing the resource potential of the enterprise, namely, the formation of competitive advantages of the enterprise, based on the stability of the production structure and the stability of the realization prices as the basis for the growth of net income from sales and profit from the main activities of the enterprise and its components: 
• material and technical: the growth in the number, value, suitability of the main productive assets of the enterprise, decrease of the specific profit from the main activity of the enterprise by units of value of fixed assets. • labor: an increase in the number of industrial and production personnel, which does not exceed the rate of growth of profitability of personnel. • information: growth of the quantity and value of intangible assets of the enterprise, the level of their involvement in production.

title: Decision-Based Portfolio Attribution II: Linking Decisions to Return Sources

detail.abstract: Paper I decomposed the active return of an equity book into named analyst and portfoliomanager decisions through a chain of counterfactual portfolios, each decision a single return. This paper asks the question Paper I left open: through which return sources did each decision contribute? Crossing the decision partition with any exact additive decomposition of instrument returns gives a grid of decision × source cells. Its row sums are the decision components of the chain and reference convention used Paper I's components under its published convention and its column sums are conventional source attribution. For a xed source construction the column margins do not depend on the decision chain, and for a xed chain the row margins do not depend on the source construction; individual cells depend on both, and that dependence is the information the grid adds. The column set has a natural default for each asset class a factor model for equities, a carrycurvespread split or exact repricing for bonds, a dollar-prot bridge for private equity but any exact decomposition on the common universe can ll it. We demonstrate the crossing on Paper I's rating-dynamics example, where the credit for omitting an analyst BUY that fell is mostly avoided style exposure while the cost of holding a downgraded name is mostly model-unexplained. Applied to Paper I's implementation of the hit-rate and outlier-capture partition, the grid separates ranking on model-unexplained return from the contributions assigned to the specied factors: a constructed BUY list with no stock-specic skill but high loadings scores well on the raw partition in a rising sector; source resolution attributes that performance predominantly to systematic exposure, and the apparent ranking advantage largely disappears when the partition is resorted on modelunexplained return. We apply the grid to xed income under two source engines, reconcile it to a commercial engine's one-day output, carry the decision rows to absolute-return long short books, and treat private equity as a boundary case in which the rows survive and the source cells are not identied. Exact accounting is not evidence of skill; the grid separates sources so that each decision can be tested against its own comparator. Renements to Paper I's conventions are stated in an appendix so that the paper is self-contained.
