detail.abstract: To achieve decarbonation, the manufacturing sector need to adopt clean production technologies to replace existing fossil fuel using ones. Accordingly, it needs to replace its existing capital stock with one using a clean technology. Considering how capital intensive the manufacturing sector is, this may happen only if the clean technology is deemed sufficiently competitive by manufacturing firms. We study how firms may choose between investing in a clean and a dirty technology. We assume that firms initially have heterogeneous productivity with the clean technology. Thus only a subset of innovators initially invest in the clean technology, triggering a learning by doing effect which in turn benefits to an increasing number of firms. In this context, we analyze the effects of a carbon tax and a subsidy to clean investments on the pace of clean technology adoption. We characterize analytically how the investment in clean and dirty capital reacts to a carbon tax and to an investment subsidy. We find that an early subsidy enhances the effect of a subsequent carbon tax. We finally evidence competitive implications, as the most productive fringe of firms benefits more from a subsidy or a carbon price

detail.abstract: Pulmonary diseases continue to be among the largest causes of morbidity and mortality globally and are a significant strain on health care systems, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Chest X-ray is a primary imaging modality, but image interpretation is not solely dependent on the image features, but on the report text combined with image interpretation. Current deep learning systems are mainly unimodal, and even the recent multimodal ones usually concatenate image and text features at shallow levels, failing to meaningfully influence their representation. In this work, we introduce MPACT, a multimodal method for classifying binary pulmonary abnormalities in pairs of radiographs and radiology reports. The proposed framework includes: (i) a parallel hybrid visual encoder designed to obtain the local texture and global structural patterns simultaneously, consisting of a custom CNN backbone and Swin Transformer branch; (ii) a domain-adapted BioBERT text encoder with handcrafted auxiliary clinical features extracted from the text of radiology reports; (iii) a bidirectional cross-modal attention fusion mechanism; (iv) a classification head that is activated by GELU and has a residual skip-connection branch; and (v) a content-aware weighted sampling strategy, which considers class imbalance and within-class clinical heterogeneity. Compared with four benchmark models, MPACT outperforms them in terms of accuracy (98.69%), precision (0.9888), specificity (0.9887), sensitivity (0.9851), F1-score (0.9870), and AUC-ROC (0.9987) on the Indiana University Chest X-Ray (IU-XRay) dataset for distinguishing between normal and abnormal cases. Each component of the architecture contributes uniquely, as confirmed by a systematic ablation study.

detail.abstract: On May 13, 2026, the Government of Venezuela announced the launch of its external debt restructuring. Several legal aspects of that process require consideration. This paper offers a general map of those aspects to help navigate the troubled waters of Venezuelan law. It does not propose a strategy for navigating that terrain, nor does it purport to resolve every legal problem it identifies. Given the complexity and unprecedented nature of Venezuela's case, this mapping is a necessary first step: it identifies the legal questions any restructuring must answer, how they relate to one another, and the order in which they must be addressed. To that end, the paper addresses the debt perimeter, particularly non-financial debt, whose exact amount should be determined through a reconciliation process under the fiscal regulations governing Venezuelan public debt. It examines the constitutional provisions governing the authority to restructure the debt after January 3, 2026, as well as Venezuela's legal framework for advancing the restructuring process. It then discusses key institutional challenges facing the debt sustainability analysis, the contractual structure of the international bonds, the impact of economic sanctions regulations and Executive Order 14373, and the legal status of PDVSA and its affiliate, Citgo. Overall, the paper's main lesson is that, on this map, hic sunt dracones: complex legal problems under Venezuelan public law, compounded by issues in New York and international law that any restructuring must also confront.

detail.abstract: Given recent controversies about the existence of a gender wellbeing gap we revisit the issue estimating gender differences across 55 subjective well-being  metrics – 37 positive affect and 18 negative affect – contained in 8 cross-country surveys from 167 countries across the world, two US surveys covering multiple years and a survey for Canada. We find women score more highly than men on all negative affect measures and lower than men on all but three positive affect metrics, confirming a gender wellbeing gap. The gap is apparent across countries and time and is robust to the inclusion of exogenous covariates (age, age squared, time and location fixed effects). It is also robust to conditioning on a wider set of potentially endogenous variables. However, when one examines the three ‘global’ wellbeing metrics - happiness, life satisfaction and Cantril’s Ladder - women are either similar to or ‘happier’ than men. This finding is insensitive to which controls are included and varies little over time. The difference does not seem to arise from measurement or seasonality as the variables are taken from the same surveys and frequently measured in the same way. The concern here though is that this is inconsistent with objective data where men have lower life expectancy and are more likely to die from suicide, drug overdoses and other diseases. This is the true paradox – morbidity doesn’t match mortality by gender. Women say they are less cheerful and calm, more depressed, and lonely, but happier and more satisfied with their lives, than men.

detail.abstract: This brief note reports the results of a survey of tax experts regarding California's Proposition 40, a proposed one-time tax on billionaire wealth. Among 105 respondents, 69.5 percent opposed the proposal, including 71.0 percent of economists and 85.0 percent of accountants. Lawyers were more supportive, with 60.0 percent favoring the tax. Open-ended responses reveal concerns about taxpayer mobility, revenue losses, valuation difficulties, and administrative costs. The results contrast with the public endorsement of the proposal by six Nobel Prize-winning economists and highlight differences in opinion among scholars who specialize in taxation. Opinions about Prop 40 embed knowledge of the relevant empirical literature, interpretation of the empirical literature, and the values of the person holding the opinion, such that differences between groups in opinion might reflect any of these factors.

detail.abstract: Successful application of artificial intelligence to improve the efficiency and accuracy of clinical diagnosis depends on improving the scope and quality of electronic medical records and providing immediately actionable and reliable advice during clinical encounters without adding to the clerical burden on the clinician. We describe a novel system that achieves these goals efficiently using Bayesian statistical methods rather than training very large neural networks on vast quantities of low-quality data. Initial experience indicates that our SmartNote system generates reliable suggestions for possible diagnoses and useful next observations. The clinician can select from these displayed options to efficiently navigate to the relevant data entry pages. A clinical series of 1,501 initial patient visits demonstrated that the clinician could generate highly structured electronic medical records with about half of the data entry actions required to type an unstructured narrative history and physical. The structured records can be added without curation into the database for statistical analysis to steadily improve system performance.

title: Narrative Completion Under Uncertainty: A Synesthetic Provenance Architecture for Epistemic Transparency in Large Language Models

detail.abstract: Large language models generate outputs in which retrieved evidence, parametric memory, and generative interpolation are fused into a single undifferentiated text stream. The consumer of this output has no mechanism for distinguishing what was found from what was generated. This paper formalizes the problem as narrative completion under uncertainty and advances a falsifiable hypothesis: that the fused stream is nonetheless separable, because the boundary between evidential grounding and generative interpolation is geometrically decidable from transformer hidden states and the intensity of interpolation is quantifiable along a continuous gradient. The proposed instrument is a synesthetic provenance decomposition in which an auxiliary classification head, running parallel to the primary language modeling head, projects the shared hidden-state representations onto a continuous provenance gradient at every token position. Drawing on the linear representation hypothesis and the approximate orthogonality of semantic subspaces in highdimensional transformer embeddings, the paper proposes that provenance attributes are recoverable from the residual stream without distorting the geometry on which the primary unembedding head depends. The architecture produces a three-channel continuous signal analogous to RGB color depth, decomposing each token's generation into retrieval-grounded (R), parametric-memory (G), and generative-interpolative (B) components. The paper connects this decomposition to directed persistent path-homology and the complement set formalism for measuring structured absence, argues that the boundary between measurement and generation in LLM output is a continuous gradient rather than a discrete threshold, presents falsification protocols including dimensionality reduction stress tests against Cover's theorem, and specifies a concrete experimental protocol for empirical validation including ground-truth labeling pipelines, ablation study designs, and proposed benchmark datasets. The central empirical prediction is the confident-interpolation signature: high interpolation magnitude coexisting with low output entropy. If the signature is recoverable from the hidden state and survives the falsification battery, the architecture is a detector of structural confabulation, the failure entropy-based tools cannot see because they read low entropy as grounding.

detail.abstract: Many lawsuits feature a separation between ownership and control: plaintiffs formally own their claims, but lawyers exercise de facto control over key decisions. Standard fee arrangements fail to align incentives. Hourly fees induce excessive effort and delay, while percentage fees induce insufficient effort and settlement at disadvantageous terms. We propose a value-added hourly compensation scheme in which the lawyer's pay is capped by the net recovery in excess of rejected settlement offers. Benchmarking against settlement offers harnesses the defendant's incentives and information about the case to mitigate agency problems between uninformed plaintiffs and their lawyers.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops the analytical foundations and academic contributions of the Philosophy of Belonging, an interdisciplinary framework proposing that entities and their capacities are constituted through organized relations without being exhaustively determined by them.


The analysis introduces five refinements: constitutive integration, recursive ontological dependence, emergence through organized constraints, multidimensional imperfect belonging, and scientifically grounded developmental evaluation. Together, these concepts explain how individual differentiation, systemic organization, and historical transformation can coexist.


The paper distinguishes three nested ontological strata—material, biological, and institutional-human—and develops an account of emergence in which reproducible constraints generate distinctive capacities while remaining materially realized.


Comparative discussions of Hegel, Whitehead, Heidegger, Morin, Habermas, Žižek, and speculative realism clarify the framework’s philosophical antecedents and its distinctive explanatory commitments.


The social implications concern the relationship between individual and collective development, institutional adaptability, freedom, recognition, and the conditions of adequate belonging. Particular attention is given to the distinction between the structural possibility of freedom and the psychological and institutional conditions required for its effective exercise.


The paper argues that the Philosophy of Belonging contributes to contemporary philosophy and social theory by integrating relational constitution, stratified emergence, imperfect belonging, and synchronic–diachronic temporality within a framework open to scientific investigation and empirical revision.

title: The Octa Model: A Multi-Lens Integrated Framework for Operational Risk Management in Technology and Cross-Industry Environments

detail.title: The Octa Model: A Multi-Lens Integrated Framework for Operational Risk Management in Technology and Cross-Industry Environments

detail.abstract:
Operational risk increasingly emerges from interactions among governance, people, processes, technology, third parties, and rapidly changing operating environments. Yet, today’s risk-management practice often remains fragmented across governance structures, risk registers, controls, monitoring, escalation, compliance, enterprise risk management (ERM), and digital tooling/technology. This article introduces the Octa Model, a conceptual eight-lens architecture designed to connect these capabilities into a single-loop operating system. The model comprises governance and accountability, risk identification and assessment, control and mitigation, risk monitoring and reporting, risk response and escalation, compliance and continuous improvement, integration with ERM, and technology and tools. The article positions the model against ISO 31000, COSO ERM, Basel operational-risk principles, the Three Lines Model, and NIST-oriented approaches, while drawing on systems theory, control theory, socio-technical systems thinking, dynamic capabilities, and risk-governance scholarship. Its contribution is not the invention of eight isolated risk-management activities, but their explicit orchestration into an execution-oriented lifecycle with feedback, escalation, enterprise alignment, and technology enablement. The article also proposes an Octa Effectiveness Score (OES) and maturity anchors as a transparent basis for future measurement and real-world validation. An illustrative fintech deployment scenario demonstrates how the eight lenses can diagnose weak coupling among ownership, controls, monitoring, escalation, and learning. The framework is also designed for potential application across technology, healthcare, manufacturing, financial services and supply-chain environments. Ultimately, the Octa Model serves as a plug-and-play conceptual architecture meant to operationalize and adapt current standards sustainably, not replace them.

Keywords: operational risk management; enterprise risk management; risk governance; socio-technical systems; digital risk; organizational resilience.

detail.abstract: Finite multivariate Gram-Charlier expansions integrate to one by construction but are hard to keep nonnegative everywhere. We study the positive counterpart of the bivariate modified multivariate Gram-Charlier (MmGC) density, the positive MmGC (PMmGC) distribution, obtained by squaring its Hermite polynomial. It is a proper density for every parameter vector and retains closed-form moments, coskewness, cokurtosis and an exact portfolio distribution. We embed it in a twostage TGARCH framework with constant or dynamic conditional correlation. A grid-based analysis at published MmGC estimates quantifies how much of the support a finite linear expansion covers with a nonnegative density. Applied to daily returns on the S&P 500 paired with the SOX semiconductor index, gold and Brent crude oil (1990-2025), the PMmGC fits the tails better and attains a higher likelihood than the positivity-restricted MmGC in every configuration, at an identical parameter count. A test of independence of the PMmGC innovations shows that higher-order spillovers matter most where correlation is weakest: for gold and oil they leave portfolio Value-at-Risk almost unchanged but roughly double the probability of a joint 1% loss and raise conditional Value-at-Risk (CoVaR) by 11-20%, whereas for the highly correlated semiconductor index correlation captures almost all joint tail risk.

detail.abstract: A market maker that shades its quotes against its inventory reveals that inventory to an observer who knows its quoting rule and the inputs to that rule. I construct an explicit attacker against an Avellaneda-Stoikov maker in an agent-based limit order book calibrated to the Binance.US bitcoin-dollar (BTC/USD) market. An attacker that is told which quotes are the maker's, observes the price the maker quotes against and the maker's horizon, and is trained on true inventory recovers that inventory exactly; with the full-book mid in place of the maker's reference price, its out-of-sample R-squared is 0.03 ± 0.35 (mean ± standard error). Averaging its observations lets the attacker partially recover a skew jittered by independent noise, but produces no detectable gain against a quantized skew. On average, quantization preserves more inventory control than removing the skew, yet each of the four widths tested between 0.75 and 1.50 standard deviations of inventory leaks information relative to a zero-skew control, and a negative out-of-sample R-squared cannot show that a defense blinds the attacker. When an attacker trades, the maker's seven-day profit falls by $108 ± 33, an effect the design cannot attribute to leakage, and at a larger quote size a symmetric one-hour strategy using true inventory does not cover its trading costs.

detail.abstract:
Background: Coverage of breast and cervical cancer screening remains low in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). We aimed to assess regional and country-level differences in breast and cervical cancer screening coverage and examine the association between individual- and country-level factors and screening uptake in SSA. 

Methods: This cross-sectional study used Demographic and Health Survey data from women aged 30–49 years in 12 countries across the four SSA regions. We estimated breast, cervical, and dual screening coverage with 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) by region and country. We used multinomial multilevel logistic regression to estimate adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% CI. 

Findings: Overall screening coverage for breast, cervical, and dual screening was 9·2%, 7·7%, and 8·2%, respectively. Breast cancer screening coverage was higher than cervical cancer screening in West Africa (11·6%, 95% CI 11·1–12·2 vs. 2·8%, 95% CI 2·6–3·1), whereas in East Africa (4·9%, 95% CI 4·6–5·3 vs. 14·0%, 95% CI 13·3–14·8) cervical cancer screening was higher. In countries that had cervical cancer screening programmes, women had higher odds of dual screening (aOR 7·3, 95% CI 2·8–19·0). Breast cancer incidence ≥30 per 100 000 was associated with higher odds of all screening outcomes, and a free cancer care policy with higher odds of cervical and dual screening. 

Interpretation​: Cervical cancer screening programmes and free cancer care policies were associated with higher screening uptake, but SSA needs multifaceted strategies that go beyond free service provision and address sociocultural barriers.

detail.abstract: Training Needs Analysis (TNA) is an important process in identifying training needs based on the gap between the competencies that employees have and the competencies needed by the organization. This chapter discusses the analysis of training needs through task/job analysis, person analysis, and competency mapping. Task/job analysis is used to identify tasks, responsibilities, performance standards, and competencies needed in a job. Person analysis focuses on individual abilities, identifying competency gaps, and determining employee development needs. Meanwhile, competency mapping is carried out to map the competencies needed and compare them with the actual competencies of employees. The results of the three analyses are used to identify competency gaps, determine the priority of needs, and formulate training needs that are in accordance with the organization's goals. The determination of training needs also needs to consider the causes of performance problems so that training is provided in a targeted manner and does not replace other interventions that are more appropriate. Thus, the systematic implementation of TNA can help organizations develop training and development programs that are more targeted, effective, and in accordance with the needs of work and employees.

detail.abstract: Ram-page: Sheep Related Injuries Requiring Hospital Treatment in Otago and Southland, New ZealandNick Keddell MBBS (orthopaedic registrar-Southland Hospital) Jack Hanlon MBChB (orthopaedic registrar- Dunedin hospital), Ryan Paganelli MD (Emergency department consultant- Southland Hospital), Amir Sandiford MBBS(orthopaedic surgeon- Southland Hospital)Purpose To describe the nature, severity, and economic burden of sheep-related injuries requiring hospital treatment in Otago and Southland, New Zealand a region in which sheep outnumber people by 30 to 1.Methods Retrospective cohort study of patients presenting to two emergency departments within Health New Zealand Otago and Southland between April 2020 and May 2025, identified using Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC) read code W55.3 ("Bitten or struck by sheep”). Recorded were; Injury type and severity, need for hospital admission and surgical intervention, responsible animal type, mechanism of injury, and associated costs to the Accident Compensation Corporation.Results Of 59 injuries, 51%  required hospital admission and 46% required surgical intervention. The lower limb was most commonly affected, consistent with the average height of a sheep and their apparent anatomical preference for the knee. The predominant mechanism of injury was headbutt (63%). Where specified, rams were responsible for 61% of injuries. One injury was inflicted by a dead sheep. Nationally, sheep-related injuries incurred NZ$98.8 million in ACC costs over the study period. Southland recorded the highest per-capita injury rate in New Zealand at 18.6 per 1,000 people.Conclusion: Sheep related trauma in Otago and Southland is a significant and underappreciated public health concern. When hospital treatment is required, it is likely to involve admission and surgical intervention. Rams can attack with great force, and inflict severe injuries, with multiple fatalities reported locally and internationally. Rogue rams should be identified and disposed of.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence projects are often prioritized according to the value and feasibility estimates. It can overestimate opportunities that appear to be commercially viable, but have no evidence, are not operationally ready or are not ready for responsible scaling, because of trust conditions. This paper introduces I-AVAM™ (Issifu AI Value Assessment Matrix), a conceptual decision matrix to evaluate the opportunities of AI with four perspectives: Business Value, AI Readiness, Confidence, and Trust. These dimensions are linked to 6 decision mechanisms, including the Evidence Multiplier™, the Trust-to-Scale Index™, the Benefit Reliability Factor™, the Awudu Convergence Index™ (ACI™), the Scale Eligibility Index™ and Blocking Gap Logic™. Since ACI™ is geometric mean, it will not be hidden by high scores in other dimensions if the others are weak. The framework differentiates between opportunity attractiveness and evidence strength, scale permission, convergence, and realized benefit reliability. The paper discusses the framework architecture, fundamental equations, scoring logic, a sample application, research propositions and a validation agenda. I-AVAM™ is not a standard for all products to be tested; it is a base line model. It is the Awudu Convergence Principle™ that it proposes: AI investments must be accelerated when Value, Readiness, Evidence and Trust converge.

detail.abstract:
Background: Menopause is associated with hormonal and metabolic alterations that may adversely affect glycaemic parameters. We investigated whether menopausal status and its transition alter HbA1c and oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)-derived measures, independently of ageing and glucose tolerance status. 

Methods: We used baseline and 9-year follow-up data from The Maastricht Study, a population-based cohort including participants with normal glucose metabolism, prediabetes or type 2 diabetes. Women were classified as pre- or postmenopausal for cross-sectional analyses and as remaining pre- or postmenopausal, or as transitioning to post-menopause for longitudinal analyses. Men served as comparator group. Glycaemic outcomes comprised HbA1c, OGTT-derived glucose measures, and HOMA2-IR. Associations were assessed using multivariable linear regression and generalized least-squares models, with estimated marginal means derived from fitted models. 

Findings: We included 4508 women (1029 premenopausal, 3479 postmenopausal) and 4571 men. In cross-sectional analysis, HbA1c was higher in postmenopausal than in premenopausal women (41.7 mmol/mol [95%CI: 40·9–42·6] vs 40.3 mmol/mol [39·3–41·2], p<0·0001), and not different from that in men (41·8 mmol/mol [41·0–42·6], p=0.87). Hormone supplementation use was associated with lower HbA1c (-0·95±0.38 mmol/mol, p=0·013), with stronger associations among women with prediabetes and type 2 diabetes (p=0.003). Postmenopausal women exhibited higher glucose concentrations throughout OGTT compared to premenopausal women. HOMA-2IR was higher in postmenopausal women in unadjusted analysis, but no longer after correction for BMI and other confounders. In longitudinal analysis, women transitioning from pre- to post-menopause (n=265) had 1·66±0·42 (p=0·0002) and 1·17±0·40 mmol/mol (p=0·01) greater increases in HbA1c than women remaining postmenopausal and men, respectively, independent of age and glucose tolerance status. 

Interpretation: Menopausal state and its transition are associated with worse glycaemic parameters, including higher HbA1c and poorer glucose tolerance, independent of ageing. These findings suggest that menopausal transition may represent a critical window for intensive glycaemic monitoring and preventive interventions to mitigate diabetes risk.

detail.abstract:
Does a gift in direct mail pay for itself? Brands assume a gift lifts engagement, but rarely test that against the gift's price. In a preregistered randomized field experiment, a $1.20 branded pocket planner added to a cold mailing did not pay for itself at this price, and it lowered response. Break-even, from cost inputs fixed before any outcome existed, required the gift to more than double Reach (a risk ratio of 2.0651); the observed ratio was 0.732 (95% Miettinen–Nurminen CI 0.603 to 0.889). The gift did not pay for itself at this price: the 95% interval lies wholly below the frozen break-even requirement — the registered prediction, and a statement about this price, not evidence of no effect. Reach (organizations that scanned the card's QR code) was 14.87% (145/975) with the gift and 20.31% (198/975) without: −5.44 percentage points (95% CI −8.81 to −2.06, Newcombe; 343 events pooled), significant against the conventional zero-effect null (two-sided p = 0.0016), though the bar, not this test, decides. Cost per organization reached nearly tripled, from $6.90 to $19.46.
1,950 US non-profit and educational organizations in donor stewardship were randomized 975 per arm, stratified on scale; 1,947 were mailed an identical role-addressed card linking to an identical digital reveal; analysis is intent-to-treat. The threshold's cost inputs were fixed before mailing; the arithmetic ran six days later (§5.3). Two of four Holm-corrected secondaries, pressed play (adjusted p = 0.016) and rescan (0.049), were also lower (hypothesis-generating only). A results-blind manuscript was registered before unblinding.
AI use: The author used Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant, in drafting and revising this manuscript and in writing and checking the analysis, figure and rendering code. The author reviewed every output, and all analyses, judgments and conclusions are the author's own. The full statement follows the Contributions section.

detail.abstract: Between 2015 and 2026, regulators across sub-Saharan Africa enacted risk-based capital frameworks for insurers. This paper argues that these reforms are often operationalised through a sequence in which the fixed capital floor is enforced first, while the risk-sensitive requirement that gives the regime its name is deferred until the data needed to calibrate it exists. Nigeria's 2025 to 2026 reform is the central case. A recapitalisation raising over one trillion naira was completed on schedule, yet the risk-based capital framework mandated by the same statute remains at the quantitative impact study stage. Kenya's experience, in which enforcement followed the enabling statute by roughly five years and two deferrals, is read as the precedent rather than the exception, and South Africa's nine-year path to Solvency Assessment and Management is read as the counter-model in which data instruments preceded the capital call. Drawing on the author's practitioner work with supervisory return templates in West Africa, the paper introduces the Statute-to-Ratio Chain, a four-link model (calibration, return design, insurer data, supervisory capacity) that locates where transitions break, together with a typology of returndesign ambiguities that produce divergent solvency ratios from identical balance sheets. Across the cases examined, the analysis indicates that data, return design and supervisory capability, rather than the legal setting of minimum capital thresholds, are the proximate constraints on the operationalisation of credible risk-based capital, and that regulators who sequence return design and data readiness ahead of capital calls are likely to reach genuine risk sensitivity sooner and at lower industry cost.

detail.abstract: Safety work is excluded from most project schedules; job hazard analysis, permits, monitoring set up, and pre-task briefings are all expected to be done, but seldom appear as an activity with a starting and ending point. When a project is behind schedule, these unscheduled tasks are usually the first to be compressed or eliminated without anyone really noticing. In this paper, I propose that the Critical Path Method (CPM) that planners already use to drive production can be used to protect safety work rather than to compress it. I review the research that correlates production pressure to accident causation, then describe the elements of CPM that are most relevant to the discussion: the critical path, total float, hard and soft logic, and the way that leads and lags can mask unsafe overlaps. I then describe three patterns that rob safety activities of time and propose five remedies. Two case studies, one a remediation excavation and the other a planned outage that includes radiological work, show the application of the remedies in the field. I close with simple measures a project can use to assess whether safety is built into its schedule. I conclude that, for all practical purposes, a schedule is indeed a safety document.

detail.abstract: In Nigeria, startups are exploring financing options beyond strictly debt and equity financing. They are exploring financing options that feature venture equity, asset-backed debt, and development finance institution ("DFI") lending. The conjunctive use of these modes of financing raises the issue of the non-exhaustive, and in certain instances, the absence of a regulatory architecture to regulate and allocate risk among financiers of hybrid-transactions. This paper saddles itself with the responsibility of examining this issue using the Metro Africa Xpress' ("MAX") $24 million equity and debt finance deal closed in January 2026 as a case study. The article also identifies structural deficiencies within the Nigerian legal jurisprudence that shape hybrid financing in Nigeria, they are: The absence of a securitization and structured finance act, governance technicalities created by the Companies and Allied Matters Act's limited minority shareholder protection and its effect on venture equity rounds by multiple parties, the need for dual registration under the Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020 and the Secured Transactions in Moveable Assets Act 2017, and the intersection between fund managers obligations an DFI contractual veto rights under the Investment and Securities Act 2025. The paper concludes with the realism of hybrid-financing taking over the financing stage in Nigeria, and a call to regulators and stakeholders to see these transactions beyond financing and must address the inadequacy of laws in this promising area. The inadequacy of laws in this area directly affects transaction lawyers, fund managers and the Nigerian capital markets jurisprudence. 2

detail.abstract: Law firms are rapidly adopting artificial intelligence, yet task-level efficiency gains do not necessarily translate into firm-level economic value. This paper proposes and develops an integrated quantitative framework that jointly models financial impact and privacy/compliance risk through deployment architecture as a shared decision variable. The financial model decomposes AI-saved attorney capacity into avoidable cost, contribution from redeployed capacity, and forgone hourly revenue, and derives a value capture rate from these pathways. The privacy model estimates architecture-specific expected loss from confidentiality, contractual, and regulatory events. Illustrative analyses across representative firm profiles show that outcomes vary substantially with billing structure, demand conditions, technology maturity, client sensitivity, and deployment architecture. Demand redeployment emerges as a principal uncertain behavioral parameter, while risk-adjusted analysis can reverse the architecture ranking implied by financial NPV alone. The framework is diagnostic rather than predictive and designed for firm-specific calibration.

detail.abstract: We study how generative AI is changing firms' demand for high-skill foreign labor, combining H-1B Labor Condition Applications for fiscal years 2020-2025 with a usagebased measure of AI exposure from the Anthropic Economic Index. We first document that foreign skilled workers are highly exposed to generative AI: 85.7 percent of H-1B positions are in the most AI-exposed quartile of occupations, and AI usage per worker in the average H-1B occupation is 6.5 times that of the average U.S. job. Since the release of ChatGPT, the total demand for foreign skilled workers has not declined, but its composition has shifted. By FY2025, filings in occupations where AI use is mostly automation are 15 percent below their FY2022 level, while filings for AI-builder positions are 37 percent above it. The shift appears in both hires for fresh graduates and experienced workers. Regression-based analysis shows that within a firm and year, filings in AI-substitute occupations fall by 12 percent relative to the firm's other filings and the decline is entirely driven by software developers. We find increases in filings and offered wages for external hires in AI-builder positions.

detail.abstract: This paper provides applied empirical validation and econometric stress-testing for Part I of the International Integrated Clearing and Settlement System (IICSS), an output-pegged Multi-CBDC Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) architecture. Utilizing a triangulated framework of Agent-Based Computational Economics (ACE), Financial Network Stress Testing (FNST), and Monte Carlo simulations across 10,000 adversarial iterations, we evaluate the system's structural resilience against macroeconomic supply shocks, systemic bank run liquidity crises, and inputlevel Oracle fraud vectors. The dynamic macroeconomic simulation confirms that under an extreme negative output shock (Δ𝑌 =-50%), the IICSS base ledger preserves monetary base invariance (𝑀 𝑝𝑒𝑎𝑘) through an endogenous velocity deceleration (𝑉(𝑡)), successfully absorbing price volatility without inducing a debt-deflation spiral. Under a 100% panic deposit withdrawal shock across a 100-bank interbank network, the 100% full-reserve constraint maintains absolute institutional solvency, yielding a Contagion Index of 𝐶𝐼 = 0.00. Furthermore, restricting passive cash holdings via a dynamic 10 × turnover cap accelerates Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) by +185% without capital flight leakage. Finally, game-theoretic Monte Carlo testing demonstrates that a 4-tier Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) physical triangulation taxonomy elevates asymmetric fabrication costs beyond prospective minting yields, driving the Systemic Loss Ratio toward zero (𝑆𝐿𝑅 → 0.00%). These findings quantitatively validate that replacing ex-nihilo credit creation with an output-bound full-reserve DLT framework secures long-term monetary and financial stability.

detail.abstract: This study examines a less explored dimension of contemporary generative artificial intelligence systems: the unequal number of tokens required by different languages to express semantically equivalent content. While tokenization is often treated as a technical preprocessing stage, in practice it directly affects computational cost, context limitations, and operational efficiency in large language model ecosystems. The empirical analysis relies on the FLORES-200 parallel corpus and the cl100k_base tokenizer implemented through the tiktoken library. Using 997 parallel observations across English, Spanish, Portuguese, German, and Simplified Chinese, an experimental dataset was constructed to evaluate token-linguistic efficiency under semantically comparable conditions. The findings reveal relatively stable differences across languages. Using English as the computational baseline, the average Token-Linguistic Inequality Index (TLII) reached 1.49 for Portuguese, 1.56 for Spanish, 1.59 for German, and 1.89 for Simplified Chinese.

detail.abstract: This paper provides an overview of evidence on firms' adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI). We revisit the main conceptual drivers of AI uptake discussed in the literature and summarize global trends in AI diffusion. We then examine the firm characteristics associated with adoption-including the distinction between in-house development and external acquisitionand highlight how patterns differ between general AI and generative AI technologies (GenAI). Next, we review the emerging literature on the productivity effects of AI, distinguishing nonexperimental firm-level studies from recent experimental and quasi-experimental evidence on task-level impacts. As a case study, we draw on recent firm-level data from the German Innovation Survey to investigate how adoption decisions correlate with firm size, age, R&D intensity, human capital, location, and strategic orientation, and how these patterns vary across stages and types of AI adoption.

detail.title: The Chiropractic Web Estate: A Cross-Sectional Audit of 50 UK Chiropractic Clinic Websites for Advertising Claims, Registration Disclosure and Technical SEO

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is founder and director of True SEO Consultants Ltd, which provides search engine optimisation and website services to healthcare practices, including chiropractic clinics, and offers clinics a free website claims check. The study was designed and is reported with this interest declared. AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic) was used for scripting, coding of claim snippets, figures and drafting, as disclosed in the report.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study used publicly available websites only, involved no human participants and publishes no personal data. Clinics are anonymised.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding. The study was carried out by True SEO Consultants Ltd.
declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: Not applicable. This is not a clinical trial.

detail.abstract: Background. UK chiropractors advertise under the CAP Code, which the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) applies to a clinic's own website, and under the General Chiropractic Council (GCC) Code of Professional Practice in force from 1 January 2026. CAP guidance names the conditions a chiropractor may claim to treat without holding further evidence. We found no peer reviewed study published since 2022 that measures how UK chiropractic clinic websites handle these claims, how they disclose registration, or how they are built for search. Methods. A cross-sectional audit of 50 clinic websites, five in each of ten UK cities, selected from web search results under written eligibility rules on 13 October 2026. Every site was crawled with Screaming Frog SEO Spider (10,337 URLs; 4,877 HTML pages returning 200). Up to 45 pages per site were then scanned for treatment claims, registration details, the Dr title and booking features (1,649 pages), and homepage structured data was parsed. Claim snippets were coded against the CAP accepted list under written rules. Results. Of 49 content scanned sites, 25 (51.0%) presented at least one condition outside the CAP accepted list as one the clinic treats, most often frozen shoulder (15 sites) or whiplash (13 sites), and 42 (85.7%) showed no GCC registration number on any page checked. Of 50 crawled sites, 40 (80.0%) had pages without a meta description; 22 of 49 homepages (44.9%) carried no LocalBusiness family structured data, 17 of 49 sites (34.7%) had no page for a single condition and 20 of 50 (40.0%) linked internally to pages returning a 4xx error. No content scanned site passed all ten core checks; the median site failed five. Conclusions. Most technical and disclosure gaps are of a kind a website template can prevent, so they can be closed once, when a site is built. Claims outside the accepted list are content decisions that no template prevents. The anonymised dataset, codebook and reproduction script are published with this report.

title: The Containment Gap: Autonomy, Detection and Loss of Control in Documented AI Incidents, 2010-2026
affiliations: Universidad del Alba

detail.title: The Containment Gap: Autonomy, Detection and Loss of Control in Documented AI Incidents, 2010-2026

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. The author has no personal or financial relationships with other people or organisations that could inappropriately influence or bias this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study uses publicly available secondary data on incidents and involves no human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific funding.

detail.abstract: Public debate about artificial intelligence (AI) that escapes the control of those who deploy it relies mostly on a handful of memorable episodes. This article measures the phenomenon systematically using the full AI Incident Database (AIID) snapshot of 12 October 2026. Loss of control is defined, without discretionary coding, through the causal taxonomy of the MIT AI Risk Repository: harm caused by the AI system itself, unintentionally, after deployment. Of 1,482 classified incidents dated 2010-2026, 660 (44.5%) meet this definition. Four pre-specified hypotheses are tested. First, the share of loss-of-control incidents did not rise; it fell from 66.1% (2010-2022) to 33.2% (2023-2026) (odds ratio per year 0.82, p < 0.001). The decline disappears once deliberate misuse is excluded (OR 0.96, p = 0.12), and the annual count of loss-of-control incidents grew by about 33% per year, so control failures were crowded out of the record by misuse rather than reduced. Second, among 178 incidents with a coded autonomy level, loss of control rises from 55.3% where a human makes the decision to 86.7% where the system acts without simultaneous human oversight (permutation p = 0.0002; OR 2.26 per autonomy level). Third, the organisation that built or deployed the system was the first public source in only 1.0% of all incidents and 3.9% of incidents in which that organisation is identifiable; the rate is lower for loss-of-control incidents (2.1% versus 5.6%), but the difference is not statistically significant (Fisher p = 0.12). Fourth, loss-of-control incidents cluster by deployer far beyond chance (311 repeat cases against 231 expected; permutation p = 0.0001), also after removing the five largest deployers. The evidence describes a containment gap: the more autonomous the system, the more likely its failures are of the loss-of-control type, and those failures are made public almost exclusively by outsiders. The implications for incidentreporting mandates such as Article 73 of the EU AI Act are discussed.

title: Decentralized Partnership Agreements and Self-Declared Tokens: A Conceptual Systematization of Self-Sovereign Identity and On-Chain Contracting
affiliations: Adam University

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that they have no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: This article proposes a procedure for forming and documenting partnership agreements between cryptocurrency wallet holders. It preserves contractual terms, participant information, and evidence identifying the agreement they accepted. A Self-Declared Token (SDT) records a participant's declaration of identity. It contains a hash computed from identity particulars entered by the participant and a banking transaction identifier. The underlying data are not published. A single SDT can be used across multiple agreements. A Decentralized Partnership Agreement (DPA) records the terms of joint activity, participants' wallet addresses, their agreed shares in rights, obligations, or economic outcomes, and acceptance of a specific agreement version. Two acceptance modes are available: a reference to an SDT, with verification that the signing wallet holds the token and preservation of a hash snapshot, or the use of previously authenticated identity information and evidence of assent linked to the same wallet and agreement version. A wallet signature without such an identification basis is insufficient under the proposed procedure. Records of an ordinary banking transaction provide an additional documentary trace for subsequent verification without requiring specialized bank integration. The central argument is that a participant seeking to protect contractual rights has a reason to preserve the ability to connect their identity to the wallet and acceptance and, if a dispute arises, to disclose the necessary particulars and documents. Comparison with digital credential systems, electronic signing services, DAO infrastructure, and general-purpose attestations identifies the model's contribution as organizing the connection between an identification basis and contractual assent, rather than creating a new cryptographic mechanism. Storing the complete agreement text on-chain permits its reconstruction independently of the original service. Recording only a hash or content identifier requires separate preservation of the document itself. SDT does not, by itself, authenticate documents, guarantee that different records refer to different individuals, or determine agreement validity. These questions are resolved through assessment of the evidence as a whole and the applicable law.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the association between a firm’s visual representation of its sustainability achievements (relative to its industry peers) or excess (sustainability) visualization and its inclusion in the Dow Jones Sustainability World Index (DJSI). Drawing on impression management research and interviews with sustainability raters, we theorize that the negative association between excess visualization and DJSI inclusion may reflect two potential mechanisms: reactance to suspected greenwashing and greater information-processing demands. We apply machine-learning image-identification methods to 430,697 images from 5,441 reports published by 2,570 firms between 2018 and 2020. In regression analyses, we compare 684 sustainability-comparable firm-year observations slightly below and above the DJSI inclusion threshold. We find evidence that images related to nature, biodiversity, and human diversity are associated with a lower likelihood of DJSI inclusion, although efforts to improve a firm’s communication credibility reduce this negative association. This paper contributes to impression management research, methods for analyzing visual content, and the influence of visualization on strategic outcomes.

detail.abstract: Account-to-account payment has not reached the physical counter in Europe, despite rails that are fast, inexpensive and, since October 2025, legally compulsory. This paper compares ten payment schemes-Bancontact, girocard, Interac, Pix, UPI, Alipay and WeChat Pay, PayNow with SGQR, BLIK, Bizum and Wero-against twenty-four governance, technical and commercial decisions fixed before any case was examined. The ten do not arrange themselves along a spectrum. They fall into two groups: schemes distributed by the institutions that already held the counter, which built no address layer and rent their cross-border capability; and schemes built to displace an incumbent, which entered away from the counter, constructed an address layer, and are growing. Three decisions separate them-where a scheme enters, whether it resolves a human-readable identifier to an account, and whether its promoter gains from adoption by some route other than the payment itself. The last of these binds hardest and is not technical. One feature is absent from every scheme examined: none carries more than a single payment instrument.

title: On Omnipolies, Scarcity and Unregulated Markets in the Digital Economy: Lessons from Counter-Strike 2
affiliations: Technion-Israel Institute of Technology and Tel Aviv University

detail.title: On Omnipolies, Scarcity and Unregulated Markets in the Digital Economy: Lessons from Counter-Strike 2

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: When one firm issues a digital asset, controls its supply and runs the secondary market where it trades, buyers own the asset only in part: the firm can change what it is worth and earns a commission on the trading that follows. We call such a firm an omnipoly and use a natural experiment to measure what its control costs holders and how one decision can tie together the prices of previously unrelated items. In October 2025, Valve Corporation, the producer of the online game Counter-Strike 2 and operator of its market, changed the rules without notice so that players could make knives and gloves, the rarest and most expensive items, out of five ordinary weapon skins. Until then, new ones could only come from lucky case openings. Within two days knife prices fell 14-26% and glove prices 22-34% relative to control items, the skins the rule uses rose 65%, and the surge in trading earned Valve an estimated $19.7 million in additional fees. The evidence suggests holders left this risk unpriced not because they ignored it but because the only way to act on it was to sell their items and leave the market. We show that the direction of these changes can be predicted from posted prices before the rule takes effect, allowing regulators to identify in advance who will be hurt. These results reveal how an omnipoly can shift value between holders while earning fees on the trading this causes, and why its commitments need enforcing.

title: Designing Return Policy in E-Commerce: A Trade-off between Purchase and Return Efficiency
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Designing Return Policy in E-Commerce: A Trade-off between Purchase and Return Efficiency

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

affiliations.org_name: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

detail.abstract: We study the effect of return policies by asking whether they encourage efficient returns and purchases. A stricter return policy curbs inefficient ex-post returns, but the resulting lower return rates make higher product prices more attractive for sellers, leading to possible exclusion of ex-ante efficient purchases. We compare automatic coverage that reimburses return-shipping costs (RI) with optional coverage (CI) by estimating a structural model of purchase, insurance, and return decisions under monopoly pricing across six apparel categories. A lenient return policy like RI performs better in high-margin, high-salvage categories by expanding valuable purchases, whereas a strict return policy like CI performs better in thinner-margin categories by curbing excessive returns. Partial RPD, a menu pairing a discounted price with a medium restocking fee as penalty, performs better than RI and CI for most categories by better balancing purchase and return efficiency.

title: Does Generative AI Substitute for Researchers?: Evidence from Academic Journal Authorship
affiliations: Korea University

detail.title: Does Generative AI Substitute for Researchers?: Evidence from Academic Journal Authorship

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract: Generative AI can perform many of the cognitive tasks that research teams divide among coauthors, but how far it reaches into the core of research differs across fields. In "dry" fields, whose core steps are symbolic (mathematics, statistics, mathematical physics, economics, political science), large language models can enter derivation, computation, analysis, and writing. In "wet" fields, whose core steps are physical manipulation and measurement (biology and chemistry), they reach mainly peripheral tasks. I use this pre-determined difference in task exposure to ask whether the release of ChatGPT bent field-level trends in research labor. The data are an OpenAlex panel of 1,118 journals and 1.70 million research articles (2015-2025), with journals classified by their 2022 Web of Science categories. Estimation uses doubly robust difference-in-differences. Team size and author career length rose in both groups over the period. Relative to wet journals and measured from 2022, the change in mean authors per paper in dry journals averaged -1.5% over 2023-2025 (not statistically significant) and reached -2.7% in 2025. For author career length, the corresponding estimates are -1.8% (significant only at the 10% level) and -3.0% to -3.7%. These estimates are preliminary. The author-count estimate is sensitive to the base year and to early pre-period differences, and whether the career gap comes mainly from faster growth in wet fields or slower growth in dry fields depends on the reference year. I discuss the main threats to identification and set out the tests that will sharpen the evidence.

detail.abstract: A management body, which includes the board, approves how much cyber risk its organization may take. Yet many decisions to accept a cyber risk are made lower down, for example when a system owner decides not to patch. Research on board oversight has focused on expertise. We ask a prior question: what must the record of such a decision contain for the board to check it? We develop a four-level conceptual model, from the information system to the management body. Authority moves down as thresholds; the risk moves up, and each level renames it. A decision can be checked from above only if its record names the higher-level risk and the threshold that applied, with its version. Of twelve texts reviewed, two partly provide the link to the higher-level risk; none requires the record to name the threshold and its version. For research on IT decision rights, what can be checked depends on what each record refers to.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No Conflict of interest

detail.abstract: Digital promotion initiatives frequently begin with social media posts or QR codes, but a visitor-facing link alone cannot guarantee accurate destination information, inclusive access, or benefits for local enterprises. This conceptual working paper proposes a low-cost digital discovery framework for Indonesian destinations, combining an agreed business-data standard, visitor entry points, human verification, and routine governance. It uses a critical desk-based synthesis of established smart-tourism literature and published Indonesian studies; no field data were collected and no new empirical impact estimates are claimed. The contribution is a practical sequence for small destinations: establish a minimum viable record, offer multiple discovery channels, designate record stewards, and audit inclusion and accessibility. A falsifiable set of propositions and a secondary-data research protocol are provided to support future validation.

detail.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) has made substantial progress in performance and usability. Yet its adoption in enterprises has been uneven, and many applications have failed to scale from prototypes to production. To help explain this uneven progress, we suggest that current enterprise GenAI systems can be interpreted as a generalized search intelligence (GSI). Such a system combines knowledge learned from large volumes of text, training that improves the selection of useful outputs, and information retrieved from databases, web searches, and connected tools to enrich the model's context. This view yields practical heuristics for how organizations should integrate GenAI into their processes.

detail.title: AI Verification Costs and the Delegation of Work

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a framework in which AI's work can be delegated only if it can be checked at a cost worth paying. I build a measure that adds verification to what AI can do and what AI is doing. I code how cheaply each task can be checked and measure the loss from mistakes. Applying the measure to US occupations, I find that less than half of the work done with AI can be delegated. The time AI saves is similar across occupations, but delegability varies widely. Occupations with more delegable work are projected to grow less. Realized labor-market outcomes do not yet show an effect of AI. These results suggest that the cost of checking AI's work, not what AI can do, limits how much work AI takes over.

detail.abstract: Punishment imposes costs, but it can also communicate meaning. Across three studies with Turkish and U.S. participants, we tested whether, and why, people engage in communicative punishment. Study 1 replicated a prior U.S. experiment and extended it to Turkey using prewritten punishment messages. Study 2 allowed participants to write and send their own messages across diverse transgression scenarios while also measuring their motives. Study 3 replicated this design and tested whether punishers believe that communication makes punishment more consequential. We found consistent results across studies and countries: 44.5% to 64.0% of participants engaged in communicative punishment, with Turkish participants communicating more often in Studies 2-3. The strongest predictor of communication was wanting the offender to understand the reason for punishment. Study 3 further showed that message senders perceived greater added value of communication than non-senders. These findings suggest that communicative punishment is robust and generalizes across Turkish and U.S. samples.

detail.abstract:
This research report proposes the HUMAN 2030 Framework (Natseva, 2026), an integrative conceptual framework of five capability domains: Technological, Cognitive, Human, Adaptive and Value-Creation Intelligence. The framework describes the capacities that sustain human value creation in an AI-intensive economy. The report introduces Professional Identity Adaptability (PIA), a proposed psychological construct: the capacity to revise one's professional self-concept, competencies, occupational role and mode of value creation as occupations change, without remaining psychologically dependent on a single fixed occupational identity. It also introduces the Occupational Human Anchoring Index (OHAI), a proposed analytical instrument that separates substitution pressure from human anchoring across eleven rated dimensions. Adaptability security is derived as an implication for how career security should be understood.

The report synthesises evidence from the IMF, ILO, OECD, World Economic Forum, Eurostat and peer-reviewed research published between 2023 and 2026. It distinguishes AI exposure, task automation, augmentation, occupational transformation, employment displacement and occupational disappearance. It includes an illustrative OHAI application to 92 occupations and emerging AI-related functions and eight testable propositions. It gives recommendations for adults at different career stages, for the education of adolescents, and for universities, employers and governments. It closes with three assumption-based scenarios for 2030, a validation research agenda and a development item pool for the Professional Identity Adaptability Scale (PIAS-DV).

All constructs are conceptual proposals and have not been empirically validated. OHAI scores are an illustrative application of the proposed framework, not empirical results.

title: Why Digital Twins Stall at the Digital Shadow: Data Lifecycle Fragmentation as the Structural Barrier to Built Environment Maturity
affiliations: University of Bristol

detail.title: Why Digital Twins Stall at the Digital Shadow: Data Lifecycle Fragmentation as the Structural Barrier to Built Environment Maturity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests relevant to this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific external funding and was supported solely by the author's institutional resources.

detail.abstract: Digital twin technology promises bidirectional, lifecycle-spanning integration between physical assets and their digital counterparts, yet empirical assessments consistently reveal that implementations stall at the digital shadow stage, characterised by unidirectional data flows and limited operational integration. This article argues that the binding constraint on digital twin maturity in the built environment is not sensing capability or technical interoperability alone, but data lifecycle fragmentation: the systematic loss of data continuity, context, and traceability across the transitions from design through construction to operation. Synthesising evidence from a systematic review of 112 built environment digital twin cases, lifecycle data integration research, and handover studies, the analysis shows that 60.7 percent of implementations cluster at Level 2 maturity, with lifecycle data coverage identified as a persistent weakness across all application domains. This pattern is produced by structural mechanisms including procurement-driven data fragmentation, phase-optimised tool ecosystems, and the absence of owner-controlled systems of record that persist beyond project completion. The article proposes that digital twin maturity assessment must be reframed to treat lifecycle data continuity as a first-order diagnostic dimension, and outlines implications for governance, information management practice, and future research. The argument challenges the prevailing narrative that digital twin immaturity is primarily a technical sensing problem and redirects attention to the organisational and contractual structures that sever the digital thread.

detail.abstract: The productive use of new technologies depends not only on formal training but also on the practical knowledge workers exchange. Professional specialties differ in the routines and norms that govern how new tools enter everyday work. We investigate whether exposure to colleagues from different specialties influences how workers apply generative AI. In a nationwide generative-AI training program involving 750 in-service teachers, we randomly assigned participants to groups of five. Groups either mixed primary, secondary STEM, and secondary non-STEM teachers or consisted of teachers from the same specialty. Curriculum, instructor, and tool access were identical across groups. At the end of the core curriculum, teachers in mixed groups reported greater use of AI in their teaching (0.19 standard deviations). The increase was driven primarily by using AI to construct grading rubrics, a relatively uncommon application before training. Estimated gains were largest among primary teachers, whose baseline AI use was relatively low, and among teachers without a same-specialty groupmate. These findings suggest that the professional culture in which workers learn a technology shapes how they apply it, and that bringing together workers from different specialties may help practices cross professional boundaries and broaden the applications of new technologies.

detail.abstract: Although price personalization can expand inclusion and access, it presents distinct challenges for consumers whose behavior is driven by constraint rather than preference. This article shows how, first, narrow-horizon thinking and compensatory coping may cause constrained consumers to deviate from rational benchmarks in ways that algorithms exploit. Second, it demonstrates how predictive and interpretive gaps can lead constrained consumers to be systematically overcharged. We consider three protective strategies: shifting the compliance burden from consumers to firms, e.g. through bans and universal privacy opt-outs, bolstering systematic accountability through algorithmic auditing, and reducing the role of constraint in purchasing contexts, through purchase interrupters, rights of return, and reference pricing.

title: On the Stability of Token Systems
affiliations: Jesse H. Jones Graduate School of Business, Rice University

detail.title: On the Stability of Token Systems

affiliations.org_name: Rice University - Jesse H. Jones Graduate School of Business

detail.abstract:
Token systems offer a market solution for non-monetary economies, where monetary transactions are undesirable or restricted. In such systems, agents request and provide services (trade favors) over time with possibly different rates, and tokens are used to pay for service provision. The stability and effectiveness of token systems depend on whether token accumulation and debts of agents can be controlled. This control becomes more challenging when the service availability is minimal. When for every service request only a few agents can provide the service, the resulting low liquidity makes it harder to reward agents for their contributions. 

We characterize necessary and sufficient conditions for the stability of token systems under the minimum token selection rule, where the agent with the minimum amount of tokens is chosen to provide service among the available providers. For homogeneous token systems in which each service costs the same amount of tokens, these conditions require that for any subset of agents, their total service request rate is strictly greater than their unavoidable token earning rate. We show that if any of these conditions is violated, no stationary provider selection rule can stabilize the system. 

We extend our characterization to systems where services are heterogeneous, i.e., the cost of each service may be random and requester dependent, and we provide explicit tail bounds on stationary token endowments of agents. Our results shed light on how much asymmetry and heterogeneity a token system can tolerate to sustain cooperation. We discuss several market design levers for the social planner, while arguing how to relate stability to full participation in an ex-ante commitment game, where agents are risk sensitive.

title: The Duration Gap: Value-at-Risk, Interest-Rate Swaps and the 2026 Losses of Chile's Most Conservative Pension Fund
affiliations: Universidad del Alba

detail.title: The Duration Gap: Value-at-Risk, Interest-Rate Swaps and the 2026 Losses of Chile's Most Conservative Pension Fund

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable: the study uses aggregate public financial data and involves no human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Between January and September 2026, Fund E, the most conservative of Chile's five mandatory pension fund types, lost about ten per cent in real terms, its second-worst result on record, while the funds' positions in foreign interest-rate derivatives swung to a reported valuation loss of about US$7.7 billion. This article asks why standard Value-at-Risk (VaR) measures did not warn of the loss. Using daily unit values for the seven pension fund administrators (AFPs) from January 2015 to October 2026, Chilean and US government yields and the exchange rate, I estimate the funds' effective duration to US long-term yields and backtest six VaR models at daily and monthly horizons. Four hypotheses were stated before estimation. First, Fund E's sensitivity to the US ten-year yield rose from about 0.2 years in 2016-2019 to 7.2 years in 2026 (change 6.3 years, z = 11.4), rising from late 2022 and accelerating from late 2023, consistent with the build-up of receive-fixed dollar swaps; US rates account for-7.9 of the-6.5 percentage points of nominal return in January-September 2026. Second, contrary to the hypothesis, daily 99% VaR models broadly met their coverage in 2026 (three to six exceptions against about two expected); the loss was a persistent drift, not a sequence of tail days. Third, an exposure-adjusted VaR, which applies the current factor exposure to a long history of rate moves, rose to 7.4% of the fund for a one-month horizon in June 2026, more than twice the 3.5% given by historical simulation scaled by the square root of time, which was then at its lowest level since early 2024; only the exposure-adjusted measure covered the September 2026 loss of 5.1%, in all seven AFPs and in nine window combinations. Fourth, differences in pre-shock exposure across AFPs did not significantly predict the size of the loss (Spearman ρ = 0.50, exact p = 0.13). The gap between what a volatility-based VaR measures and what the portfolio is exposed to supports the stress-based derivatives limit that the regulator introduced in April 2026.

title: Machine Learning in Asset Pricing

detail.title: Machine Learning in Asset Pricing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors do not have any personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced this study.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was not funded by a specific organization.

affiliations.org_name: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta
Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School
Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School

detail.abstract: This survey reviews selected machine learning methods in asset pricing in two parts. The first part focuses on time-series predictability of the aggregate stock market excess return, covering recent advances such as the “virtue of complexity,” the “virtue of noise,” and the single optimal factor of predictors. We also discuss other new methods and novel predictors, including return decomposition, forecast-agnostic portfolios, option-based bounds, macro-financial trends, and large language model (LLM)-based textual signals. The second part examines cross-sectional stock return predictability and efficient portfolio estimation. Starting from the Fama-MacBeth framework and key performance measures, we survey recent developments such as LASSO regularization, forecast combination and encompassing, heterogeneous return response models, constrained deep learning, genetic programming, feasible stochastic discount factor estimation under portfolio constraints, and LLM applications to numerical financial data. Overall, the evidence strongly supports return predictability, with machine learning methods delivering substantial gains vis-à-vis conventional benchmarks.

title: Due Care in the Age of Automation Hype: Protecting the Cyber Commander's Judgment
affiliations: University of Liverpool

detail.title: Due Care in the Age of Automation Hype: Protecting the Cyber Commander's Judgment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: A senior cyber commander's judgment is tested between press alarm and promised productivity gains from automation. Artificial intelligence agents entered systems of a technology company and an Australian government agency without authorisation, and both incidents were recognised late. In offensive and defensive operations, the commander must be able to say who authorised an action, within what restrictions, who could stop it, and how its effect was assessed. This conceptual article maps the six phases of NATO's joint targeting cycle onto the defender's work on a vulnerability. It then tests the map against exploit benchmarks, incident reports, and patching studies. A benchmark speaks to one phase: the building of an exploit. The theory of constraints explains why faster discovery does not speed removal when the step after it is already saturated: findings wait. Where inventories are reliable, this article expects that step to be human, an analyst's validation or an officeholder's decision to change a mission system. Testing, vendor support, or verification may be the limit instead, and paired measures with a measurement protocol show which. Acceleration helps only where it reaches the saturated step. An adversary that answers to no one skips the limits of authorisation and approval. The accountable commander cannot. A record of due care, kept before an incident, lets the commander show afterwards what judgment was exercised. The article extends operation assessment in cyber defence from incidents to the routine flow of findings and changes.

title: Assessing the Influence of HIS Implementation on Program Effectiveness in Primary Healthcare Organizations: Evidence from RHUs in Region II, Philippines

University of Batangas, Batangas City, Philippines

detail.abstract: Health Information Systems (HIS) play a critical role in supporting health program management through improved data management, patient monitoring, and evidence-based decision-making. This study examined the level of HIS implementation and the effectiveness of program management among Rural Health Units (RHUs) in Region II, Philippines. Using a quantitative descriptive-correlational research design, data were collected from 83 municipal health office personnel from RHUs across Region II. Frequency, percentage, weighted mean, and Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient were used in data analysis. Analysis revealed that HIS implementation was generally favorable across RHUs in Region II. Program effectiveness was rated highly across case identification, patient enrollment, patient monitoring, follow-up management, and program planning and evaluation. A very weak positive relationship was observed between HIS implementation and program effectiveness; however, the relationship was not statistically significant. The study identified infrastructure and human resource constraints as the major challenges affecting HIS implementation. Based on these findings, the study developed a proposed action plan to strengthen HIS implementation and enhance program effectiveness. The study contributes to applying the DeLone and McLean Information Systems Success Model in primary healthcare settings by showing that favorable HIS implementation alone does not necessarily translate into improved program effectiveness and that organizational, human resource, and infrastructure factors remain critical to realizing system benefits. The findings further offer practical advice to policymakers, local government units, and RHU administrators in strengthening digital health governance, workforce capacity, infrastructure, and overall program performance.

title: The AI Confidence Trap When Fluent Advice Outruns Reliable Evidence
affiliations: Independant researcher

detail.title: The AI Confidence Trap When Fluent Advice Outruns Reliable Evidence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known financial or personal relationships that could have influenced the research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a conceptual paper based on published literature and does not involve human participants, personal data collection, or experimental procedures.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence can produce advice that is fast, coherent, specific, and persuasive even when its evidential basis is weak. This article identifies the AI Confidence Trap: a reliance-calibration failure in which decision-makers treat presentation confidence as a proxy for decision competence. The trap does not describe a new universal bias, nor does it imply that managers should distrust AI. It integrates evidence from large-language-model experiments, algorithm-advice research, and documented organizational failures to explain why fluent answers can receive more authority than their reliability warrants. The article distinguishes presentation confidence, validated uncertainty, and decision competence; identifies the conditions under which these dimensions are most likely to diverge; and introduces a Confidence-Competence Diagnostic for managerial use. It then develops five governance routines: separating style from evidence, designing verification friction, exposing uncertainty and limits, making reliance and overrides observable, and matching controls to decision risk. The central managerial objective is calibrated reliance-accepting correct and useful AI advice, resisting incorrect or contextually incomplete advice, and abstaining when evidence is insufficient. The article concludes that organizations should evaluate decision-support AI not only by adoption and efficiency, but also by whether human reliance changes appropriately as system reliability changes.
